hits.title: [Frontend] [Parser] Migrate llama3_json/llama4_json to the streaming parser engine
hits.body:
# Purpose `llama3_json` streaming and non-streaming disagree: the legacy parser re-parses a cumulative buffer with fixed separator arithmetic, so at more than one token per SSE delta it returns tool calls that do not parse — **174/858 valid at 5 tokens/delta (20.3%), against 858/858 here**. This migrates `Llama3JsonToolParser` (registry names `llama3_json`, `llama4_json`) onto the declarative `ParserEngine`, where non-streaming replays the same state machine as streaming, so the two agree by construction. It also un-breaks `llama4_json`, which raised at construction on real Llama-4 tokenizers. | tokens per SSE delta | legacy, valid JSON | legacy, AST-correct | this branch, valid JSON | this branch, AST-correct | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | 849/858 (99.0%) | 379/858 (44.2%) | **858/858 (100.0%)** | **672/858 (78.3%)** | | 2 | 405/858 (47.2%) | 166/858 (19.3%) | **858/858 (100.0%)** | **672/858 (78.3%)** | | 5 | 174/858 (20.3%) | 62/858 (7.2%) | **858/858 (100.0%)** | **672/858 (78.3%)** | Measured live, **streaming**, on the full BFCL v4 set (858 cases, `simple_python`/`live_simple`/`multiple`): each parser's exact generated tokens replayed through `extract_tool_calls_streaming` at 1/2/5 tokens/delta, scored with `bfcl-eval`'s own `ast_checker`. This branch is flat across every chunk size — not just "still valid JSON" but "still the right call" — matching the 78.1% non-streaming weighted accuracy in the eval section below.
Reproducing the headline table ```bash pip install "bfcl-eval>=2025.10.20.1,<2026" vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --max-model-len 8192 \ --served-model-name localmodel --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser llama3_json .venv/bin/python bfcl_stream_replay.py ``` Download [bfcl_stream_replay.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33303165/bfcl_stream_replay.py) To score legacy the same way: swap the checkout (unmodified `main`), run with **that checkout's own `.venv/bin/python`**, and add `--tool-call-parser legacy_llama3_json`.
Model eval — official bfcl-eval, live, n=858 Ran `bfcl-eval==2025.12.17.1` directly against two separate live `vllm serve` instances, **non-streaming** (`bfcl-eval` does one-shot generation), same model, greedy decoding, same 858 BFCL **v4** test cases — `simple_python`, `live_simple`, `multiple`, the full category files the package ships, not a subsample: this branch with `--tool-call-parser llama3_json` on one GPU, and the real pre-migration `Llama3JsonToolParser` — an unmodified current-`main` checkout, where the registry still resolves `llama3_json` to the legacy class — on a second GPU. | category | n | legacy (pre-migration) | this branch | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | non-live simple (Python) | 400 | 41.50% | **83.00%** | | non-live multiple | 200 | 32.00% | **80.50%** | | live simple | 258 | 52.33% | **68.60%** | | weighted average | 858 | 42.5% | **78.1%** | **Reproducing this table:** ```bash pip install "bfcl-eval>=2025.10.20.1,<2026" vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --max-model-len 8192 \ --served-model-name localmodel --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser llama3_json .venv/bin/python bfcl_nonstream.py ``` Download [bfcl_nonstream.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33303180/bfcl_nonstream.py) Expect the per-category accuracies above (± minor model/hardware noise); Scores land in `./score/data_non_live.csv` and `./score/data_live.csv`. Swap the checkout (unmodified `main`, where the registry still resolves `llama3_json` to the legacy class) to score the legacy parser the same way — no flag change needed.
*AI assistance was used in preparing this change (Claude Code): adversarial review, rebase analysis and test-harness work. I have reviewed every changed line and run every test reported below.* **Scope: 14 files, `+4837/-380`** (`+1837/-380` excluding tests). `llama_json.py` itself is **779 lines** — down from an earlier 1532/1438, after moving the generic resumable/truncated-JSON scanning and schema-coercion-safety splicing out to `vllm/parser/json_scan.py`, `vllm/parser/utils.py`, and `vllm/tool_parsers/utils.py`, where the same machinery is available to every parser, not just this one. **No behaviour changes for any other parser** — the `engine/` files touched register this parser's adapter and gain a config flag (`tool_call_ends_on_args_balance`) that defaults to `False` and whose only setter is `llama_json.py`.
Design The LLama JSON format is a bare envelope with no wrapper and no end marker: ``` [<|python_tag|>]{"name": "f", "parameters": {...}}; {"name": "g", ...} ``` Most tool-call formats tell the engine where a call starts and ends for free. Qwen3 wraps a call in `...`. Granite has no closing token, but `` still marks the start, and the body is one JSON array the engine already knows how to split. Llama's `<|python_tag|>` is optional, and when present isn't always followed by JSON — the model can put ordinary ipython-style text after it — so it isn't trusted as an opener the way Granite's marker is; the engine just consumes it as text and waits to see what actually follows. `{` ends up doing the opener's job instead: it's both the opener and ordinary text (prose can contain one too), and the call ends only when the JSON balances. Llama's bare envelope doesn't match an existing engine mode, so this parser answers four questions those other formats get for free: - **When does tool call ends** When the JSON balances - a new engine flag `tool_call_ends_on_args_balance` rather than a closing terminal, so separators (`;`, a newline) don't matter. - **What's the tool name, and what are its arguments** The envelope's top level `"name"` key (not one nested in the arguments), `arguments/parameters` are the model's own text, not a rebuilt JSON object - so the client sees exactly what the model wrote. - **What if the model never finishes the JSON** Cut back to the longest prefix that's still valid and closed by appending - never by rewriting text already streamed. - **What if it looks like a call but it isn't** A balanced `{...}` with no top-level `"name"` key is prose. Its events are retracted and the text restored as content. Implementation notes: - Separators `;`, newlines, commas, a second `<|python_tag|>`, or nothing at all (the xgrammar `llama` structural tag for `tool_choice="required"` forces back-to-back `{...}{...}`) all work, since the parser isn't looking for one. - The top-level `"name"` lookup is a structural scan, not the engine's regex fallback, which would match a `"name"` nested inside `parameters`. - A prose `{...}` that gets retracted has its slot recycled, so real calls still stream with dense indices from 0. - `tool_choice="required"` and named choice are handled by this parser directly (`supports_required_and_named = False`), as the other engine parsers do. - `llama_tool_parser.py` is gutted in place to an adapter shim keeping the class name and `structural_tag_model="llama"`, so the registry needs no change.
Behaviour changes vs the legacy parser (9) Each is forced by streaming/non-streaming unification or is a strict improvement. Every example is measured: the same input fed to `origin/main`'s `Llama3JsonToolParser` and to this branch. `CALL` abbreviates `{"name": "f", "parameters": {"a": "x"}}`. 1. **Leading prose before a call is returned as content** (legacy: `content=None`); text after the first completed call is still dropped. ```text in Let me check. CALL legacy f({"a": "x"}) content=null new f({"a": "x"}) content="Let me check." ``` Legacy *streaming* is worse than its own non-streaming result here — it never detects the call at all: ```text legacy (streaming) no call, content = the entire string new (streaming) f({"a": "x"}) content="Let me check." ``` 2. **An envelope needs `parameters`/`arguments` next to `name` to be a call.** Name-only and prose user-data shapes stay content — unchanged from legacy, and listed because it is a refusal worth preserving. ```text in {"name": "John", "age": 30} legacy non-streaming: content = input, no call legacy streaming: a tool call named "John" with empty arguments new both: content = input, no call ``` Non-streaming this is unchanged from legacy. Streaming, legacy promotes the user's own data to a tool call — the migration removes that by construction. 3. **Valid `name` + malformed params → a call whose arguments are cut back to the longest closeable prefix**, so they always parse. See "One deliberate deviation" below. ```text in {"name": "f", "parameters": {"a": "x", bad}} legacy no call, whole string as content new f({"a": "x"}) ``` 4. **A valid call followed by a bad object no longer drops the valid call** (#49923's bug 2 — legacy was all-or-nothing). ```text in CALL I used {searchTool} here legacy no call, whole string as content new f({"a": "x"}) ``` 5. **Arguments are the verbatim model span**, not `json.dumps` re-serialisation — same JSON value, the model's own whitespace. ```text in {"name": "f", "parameters": {"a": "x"}} legacy f({"a": "x"}) new f({"a": "x"}) ``` 6. **The constructor no longer raises when `<|python_tag|>` is absent.** This un-breaks `llama4_json`, which was unusable at startup on real Llama-4 tokenizers. ```text in Llama-4 tokenizer (no <|python_tag|> in vocab) legacy RuntimeError: could not locate the bot token '<|python_tag|>' new constructs, and parses <|python_start|> ... <|python_end|> ``` 7. **Truncated mid-JSON generation emits the partial arguments, repaired to valid JSON, in both modes.** A real generation cut at `max_tokens=16`: ```text in {"name": "get_weather", "parameters": {"location": "Boston legacy non-streaming: no call, raw partial as content legacy streaming: get_weather({"location": "Boston"}) <- and so disagrees with itself new both: get_weather({"location": "Boston"}) ``` Legacy streaming also hands the client arguments that do not parse at all, at other truncation points — `{"query": "ll` from a real `max_tokens=20` run, and 14 of 80 cells in the workload below. 8. **Prose containing braces is preserved byte-identically in streaming too.** ```text in Code: if (x) { y(); } done legacy content = input new content = input ``` 9. **Argument values are coerced to their declared schema type, and only when the value is invalid for it.** Legacy did no coercion at all; the shared engine coerces unconditionally and so corrupts already-valid values, so this guard is what keeps it from being a regression. Largest measured difference in the eval below. ```text in {"name": "f", "parameters": {"n": "10"}} with n: integer legacy f({"n": "10"}) <- str where the schema says int new f({"n": 10}) ``` Legacy streaming additionally advanced a fixed two characters past each parsed call (`start_idx += end_idx + len("; ")`), so any separator those two characters do not cover silently dropped every call after the first (#49923's bug 1): ```text in CALL;CALL (bare ";", not "; ") legacy 1 of 2 calls new 2 of 2 calls ```
## Test Result | suite | result | | --- | --- | | `tests/parser/engine/test_llama_json.py` | **590 passed** | | `tests/parser/` | **7089 passed** | | `tests/tool_parsers/` (excl. gated-tokenizer test below) | **1184 passed**, 1 skipped, 30 xfailed | | `tests/tool_parsers/test_llama3_json_tool_parser.py` | not re-run on this exact branch (gated `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct` tokenizer, no network/token in this environment); previously 14 passed, unaffected by a pure internal refactor | | #47562 regressions + no-reasoning-parser safety cases | **27 passed** (10 core #47562, 6 Llama serving-path marker, 11 Inkling shared-marker) | | `pre-commit` incl. `mypy` | clean |
Test Plan (commands) ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/parser -q .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/tool_parsers -q \ --ignore=tests/tool_parsers/test_llama3_json_tool_parser.py \ --ignore=tests/tool_parsers/test_cohere_command_tool_parser.py .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/tool_parsers/test_llama3_json_tool_parser.py -q .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files .venv/bin/pre-commit run mypy --hook-stage manual --files ``` Plus a live server on `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` for streaming/non-streaming parity, an offline `llama4_json` check against a real Llama-4 tokenizer, and a BFCL replay comparing both parsers on identical generated tokens.
On the size of the test file `tests/parser/engine/test_llama_json.py` is 2764 lines, the largest in `tests/parser/engine/`. Several things make that a budget rather than a red flag: - **`llama_json.py` itself is 779 lines**, not the 1532/1438 it was earlier in this PR's history — the generic resumable/truncated-JSON scanning (`scan_json_value`, `ValueScan`, `KeyScan`/`scan_top_level`, `closeable_prefix`, `object_members`, `array_items`, none of which reference tool calls or Llama tokens) and the verbatim-preserving schema-coercion splicer moved to `vllm/parser/json_scan.py`, `vllm/parser/utils.py`, and `vllm/tool_parsers/utils.py` — shared infrastructure now available to every engine parser, not bespoke complexity scoped to this file. What's left is the actual Llama-specific state machine. - **`llama_json` is excluded from the shared replay harness by design.** `test_replay.py:77` and `test_delegating_replay.py:97` skip it because a bare-JSON format has no `TOOL_END` terminal (mistral opts out for the same reason), so this file carries replay coverage the other parsers get for free. The opt-out is not silent: llama_json samples are still built and validated against the real parser at `chunk_size=1`. - **14 of its 24 classes are regression guards**, each traceable to a bug fixed on this branch or to an upstream issue (#49923, #47562, #45795).
## One deliberate deviation worth flagging Behaviour change 3 — a malformed or truncated envelope with a valid `name` is **promoted to a tool call** with its arguments cut back to the longest parseable prefix, where legacy failed closed and returned content. This follows the contract the other engine parsers already implement, and the alternative is worse: rejecting the call at close means withholding the tool name until the envelope balances, which removes incremental argument streaming for every Llama call, not just malformed ones. I have taken that as the right trade. If maintainers prefer failing closed for this parser specifically, say so and I will implement it — it is a contained change, and it is the only decision here I would expect to be contentious.
Other known limitations - **Named tool choice can return the whole envelope as the arguments** for schemas that constrain the object, when `VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING=0` removes the structural tag and the model emits the envelope anyway. What prevents that is the decoding grammar, and it is backend-dependent: xgrammar rejects the envelope for a typed schema, llguidance 1.7.6 at vLLM's defaults accepts it unless `disable_additional_properties` is set. Default configuration (strict on) is unaffected. - The equivalent coercion guard for `ParserEngine._coerce_value`, which would affect the other engine parsers, is deliberately not in this PR — attempted once during the size-reduction pass and reverted when it broke gemma4's and deepseek_v32's own tests, which pin different, deliberate best-effort coercion behavior. Left as a narrowly-scoped follow-up PR with full cross-parser coverage.
Interaction with the Rust frontend vLLM ships a second `llama3_json` implementation for the Rust frontend (`rust/src/parser/src/tool/json/llama.rs`), registered for both `llama3_json` and `llama4_json`. **This PR does not touch it** — after this lands the two differ under `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND`, and no CI job compares them (the Rust Frontend Cargo job only runs on `rust/` changes). Happy to mirror the behavior there in a follow-up if maintainers want the two to agree.
Duplicate-work check Per the contributing guide; re-checked against current `main` on 2026-10-11. - #44873, the feature request this PR implements, is **closed**; no new PR has opened against this area since #51577 itself. - **#48295** and **#49923** patch the same bugs by editing the code this PR deletes — not duplicates (migration vs. targeted patch), both still **open**, and will conflict on merge since the bugs they fix become structurally impossible here. - #47562 is merged and already included through `main`. **#42210** (streaming drops content on a stop-string interrupt) is incidentally fixed for `llama3_json` by this migration but stays **open**, since it isn't fixed for the other legacy parsers.

hits.title: [Core] Add MRV2 virtual-batch PCP for MLA
hits.body:
## Summary

Adds an MRV2 virtual-batch implementation for prefill context parallelism (PCP), initially targeting MLA and sparse MLA.

- Add a stateful `PCPManager` that partitions the globally scheduled MRV2 `InputBatch` into rank-local virtual rows while preserving global request state for restore, logits, and postprocessing.
- Add MRV2 input-batch plumbing for PCP positions, sequence lengths, logits indices, and hidden-state restoration.
- Add MLA PCP execution support while keeping PCP and DCP responsibilities orthogonal.
- Add sparse MLA cache insertion for GLM/DSA-style models.
- Align context-parallel group construction and KV ownership with the orthogonal PCP/DCP design.
- Update scheduler/offload tests for DCP-owned KV sharding and add concurrent GSM8K eval configurations for TP2+PCP2+EP and TP1+PCP4+EP.

## PCP algorithm

The scheduler continues to produce one global batch. Immediately before input preparation, `PCPManager` converts that batch into the rank-local virtual batch containing a portion of each prefill for that PCP rank.

Each prefill request is partitioned independently. Decode rows are replicated across PCP ranks so their model and KV-cache state remain synchronized.

### DualChunkSwap partitioning

PCP uses a DualChunkSwap-style partition to balance causal-attention work. A request is split into `2 × PCP` contiguous chunks, and rank `r` receives chunks `r` and `2 × PCP - 1 - r`.

For PCP=4:

```text
Global prefill:  | C0 | C1 | C2 | C3 | C4 | C5 | C6 | C7 |

PCP rank 0:        C0                                 C7
PCP rank 1:             C1                       C6
PCP rank 2:                  C2             C5
PCP rank 3:                       C3   C4
```

Earlier chunks attend to shorter prefixes, while later chunks attend to longer prefixes. Pairing one early and one late chunk gives each rank a more balanced amount of attention work than assigning one contiguous quarter of the request.

`K` and `V`—or latent KV in the case of MLA—are all-gathered so each rank has the full KV needed for KV-cache insertion and attention computation.

After model execution, hidden states are gathered and restored to global scheduled-token order before logits, sampling, and postprocessing.

## Orthogonal PCP and DCP groups

Parallel-group behavior now follows [RFC #46358: Unify Context Parallelism in vLLM (PCP ⊥ DCP)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/46358).

PCP and DCP are treated as independent axes:

- TP shards model heads.
- PCP partitions prefill computation.
- DCP shards KV ownership.
- KV shard count is now `DCP`, not `PCP × DCP`.

This is to make it easier to reason about:

> The reason I like this interface is that it keeps vllm/distributed/parallel_state.py cleaner/simpler, and makes it easier for the user to understand that the number of KV shards is simply dcp_size. This makes it a bit easier to reason about the KV replication factor (just becomes num_gpus / min(tp, num_kv_heads) / dcp, so its easy to know if its MLA and I want no replication I do DCP = num_gpus.

(See https://vllm-dev.slack.com/archives/C09JHEC74PM/p1771054846767689?thread_ts=1769445634.668079&cid=C09JHEC74PM for full motivation.)

For TP=2 and PCP=2:

```text
                 TP0       TP1
              +---------+---------+
PCP0          | rank 0  | rank 1  |
              +---------+---------+
PCP1          | rank 2  | rank 3  |
              +---------+---------+

TP groups:        [0, 1]  [2, 3]
PCP groups:       [0, 2]  [1, 3]
DCP = PCP:        [0, 2]  [1, 3]
DCP = TP × PCP:   [0, 2, 1, 3]
```

DCP groups span the PCP axis first and then TP. This supports the RFC’s two combined configurations:

- `DCP = PCP`: ranks already share the same TP-local query heads, so no TP query gather is required.
- `DCP = TP × PCP`: queries are gathered across TP before attention, and the combined output is restored to each rank’s TP-local heads.

Block sizing, block tables, slot mappings, prefix-cache accounting, and KV capacity scale with DCP ownership only. PCP alone partitions prefill compute and does not reduce per-GPU KV capacity.

## Results

Measured with `nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4` on 4xB300 GPUs, `--max-model-len 131072`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 32768`, eager execution, and FP8 KV cache.

The GSM8K column is a **100-sample, 5-shot smoke check only**, not the full GSM8K evaluation. The 100k TFTT value is mean TTFT across three sequential requests with exactly 100,000 input tokens and one output token. 

| Deployment | GSM8K (100 samples) | 100k TFTT | KV/GPU | KV token capacity | 131k contexts |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TP1+PCP4+EP4 | 93% | **2.859s** | 87.29 GiB | 1,964,800 | 14.99 |
| TP1+PCP4 | 93% | 3.996s | 84.37 GiB | 1,899,200 | 14.49 |
| TP2+PCP2+EP4 | 93% | 3.549s | 114.10 GiB | 2,568,320 | 19.59 |
| TP2+PCP2 | 94% | 4.773s | 115.08 GiB | 2,590,528 | 19.76 |
| TP4+EP4 | 92% | 4.746s | 127.40 GiB | 2,867,776 | 21.88 |
| TP4 | **95%** | 6.015s | **130.48 GiB** | **2,937,024** | **22.41** |

## Reproduction

Run one deployment at a time on 4xB300. The benchmark host used the following common environment:

```bash
export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
export VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=INFO
export MODEL=nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4
export VLLM_DISABLE_LL_BF16_ROUTER=1
```

```bash
# TP1+PCP4+EP4
DEPLOYMENT_ARGS=(--prefill-context-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel)

# TP1+PCP4
DEPLOYMENT_ARGS=(--prefill-context-parallel-size 4)

# TP2+PCP2+EP4
DEPLOYMENT_ARGS=(--tensor-parallel-size 2 --prefill-context-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel)

# TP2+PCP2
DEPLOYMENT_ARGS=(--tensor-parallel-size 2 --prefill-context-parallel-size 2)

# TP4+EP4
DEPLOYMENT_ARGS=(--tensor-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel)

# TP4
DEPLOYMENT_ARGS=(--tensor-parallel-size 4)
```

Start the server:

```bash
.venv/bin/vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --enforce-eager \
  --max-model-len 131072 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 32768 \
  --safetensors-load-strategy prefetch \
  --moe-backend flashinfer_cutlass \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --disable-uvicorn-access-log \
  --port 8000 \
  --seed 0 \
  "${DEPLOYMENT_ARGS[@]}"
```

Run the three-request 100k TFTT measurement:

```bash
.venv/bin/vllm bench serve \
  --backend vllm \
  --model "$MODEL" \
  --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 100000 \
  --random-output-len 1 \
  --random-range-ratio 0 \
  --num-prompts 3 \
  --max-concurrency 1 \
  --request-rate inf \
  --port 8000 \
  --ignore-eos \
  --disable-tqdm
```

Run the 100-sample GSM8K smoke check:

```bash
.venv/bin/python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py \
  --num-questions 100 \
  --num-shots 5 \
  --max-tokens 256 \
  --port 8000 \
  --temperature 0 \
  --seed 42 \
  --max-concurrency 16
```

Focused regression tests:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/attention/test_attention_splitting.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_batch_ordering.py -q

.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py::test_split_indexer_prefill_chunks -q
```

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used to draft and implement this change. The submitter reviewed the changed lines and ran the tests and model evaluations documented above.

hits.title: Scheduler: skip KV-blocked requests to prevent blocking (#31731)
hits.body:
## Purpose

Skip KV-blocked waiting requests to prevent head-of-line blocking under KV-cache pressure, fixing issue #31731.

**Motivation:** In multi-tenant inference workloads, a KV-heavy request (e.g., long context) at the head of the WAITING queue can repeatedly fail KV allocation and block all lighter requests behind it. This creates head-of-line blocking that inflates tail latency for the entire system.

**Without this fix:**
- A single KV-heavy request blocks the entire WAITING queue
- Lighter requests that could be scheduled immediately are forced to wait
- Tail latency (p99/p100) spikes unpredictably under KV pressure
- Multi-tenant workloads suffer unfair resource distribution
- System throughput degrades even when capacity exists for smaller requests

**Example of the problem:**
```
WAITING queue: [HeavyReq(needs 1000 blocks), LightReq1(needs 10), LightReq2(needs 10)]
Available KV blocks: 50

Current behavior (BUG):
  Step 1: HeavyReq fails allocation → STOP scheduling → LightReq1, LightReq2 blocked
  Step 2: HeavyReq fails again → STOP → still blocked
  Step N: HeavyReq finally gets blocks → LightReq1, LightReq2 finally scheduled
  Result: Light requests waited N steps unnecessarily ❌

With this fix:
  Step 1: HeavyReq fails allocation → SKIP → LightReq1 scheduled ✅
  Step 2: HeavyReq fails again → SKIP → LightReq2 scheduled ✅
  Step 3: HeavyReq gets blocks → scheduled ✅
  Result: Light requests scheduled immediately, no blocking ✅
```

**With this fix:**
- KV-blocked requests are skipped for the current scheduling step
- Lighter requests behind them can proceed immediately
- Skipped requests are retried at the head of the queue in the next step
- No request starvation — heavy requests still get priority retry
- Tail latency stabilizes under KV pressure

| Scenario | Before (Bug) | After (Fix) |
|----------|--------------|-------------|
| KV-heavy request at head | Blocks entire queue | Skipped, retried next step |
| Light requests behind | Forced to wait | Scheduled immediately |
| Tail latency under pressure | Spikes unpredictably | Stable |
| System throughput | Degraded | Maintained |
| Request starvation | N/A | Prevented (head retry) |

## Implementation

The fix introduces a **single, deterministic change** in the WAITING scheduling loop:

```python
# When KV allocation fails for a waiting request:
if new_blocks is None:
    # Skip this request for current step, retry next step
    request = self.waiting.pop_request()
    skipped_waiting_requests.add_request(request)
    continue  # Try next request in queue
```

| Requirement | Implementation |
|-------------|----------------|
| Skip KV-blocked requests | Pop from waiting, add to skipped list |
| Retry on next step | Skipped requests re-queued at tail (FCFS) |
| No starvation | Requests always retried, just delayed one step |
| No new config flags | Zero configuration surface |
| No new counters | Zero observability overhead |
| Deterministic behavior | O(1) skip operation, no heuristics |

**Changes:**
- `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`: Add skip logic when `new_blocks is None`
- `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py`: Add regression test for KV fairness

## Backward Compatibility

Fully backward compatible:
- No API changes
- No configuration changes
- No behavior change when KV allocation succeeds (common case)
- Existing preemption logic unchanged
- All existing tests pass

## Test Plan

```bash
# Run the new KV fairness regression test
pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_skip_kv_blocked_waiting_request_allows_light_request -v

# Run full scheduler test suite
pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py -v

# Run engine core tests
pytest tests/v1/engine_core/ -v
```

## Test Result

**New regression test: `test_skip_kv_blocked_waiting_request_allows_light_request`**

This test validates:
1. Create a heavy request that will fail KV allocation
2. Create a light request that can succeed
3. Schedule — heavy request skipped, light request scheduled
4. Next step — heavy request retried and scheduled

```
PASSED tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_skip_kv_blocked_waiting_request_allows_light_request
```

**Existing test suite:**
- All scheduler tests pass ✅
- All engine-core tests pass ✅
- No regressions in preemption behavior ✅
- No request drops or incorrect reordering ✅

## Impact

| Metric | Expected Change |
|--------|-----------------|
| p50 latency | No change (common case unaffected) |
| p99 latency | Improved (no HOL blocking) |
| p100 latency | Improved (light requests not blocked) |
| Throughput | Improved under pressure |
| Memory usage | No change |

## Why This is the Minimal Fix

This PR intentionally applies **the smallest possible change** that resolves #31731:

- The issue arises **only** when KV allocation fails for a WAITING request
- The fix **only** skips that specific request for that specific step
- Skipped requests are immediately retried on the next step (no starvation)
- No new state, counters, or configuration required
- The common case (KV allocation succeeds) is completely unchanged
- The change is deterministic, O(1), and adds no measurable overhead

Anything smaller would fail to address the issue; anything larger would violate the project's design constraints.

Fixes #31731

hits.title: [Feature]: Per-priority observability for --scheduling-policy priority
hits.body:
Body:

### 🚀 Feature request

Priority scheduling (`--scheduling-policy priority`) is supported and actively
improved (preemption ordering, KV-cache eviction, admission control, etc.), but
there is currently **no way to observe it**: all finished-request metrics
(`vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds`, `vllm:request_queue_time_seconds`,
`vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds`, `vllm:request_success`, ...) are aggregated
across all requests, with no priority dimension.

Without per-priority breakdown, an operator routing latency-sensitive traffic at
high priority cannot answer basic questions:

- Do priority -1 requests actually see lower queue time / E2E latency?
- What is the traffic mix per priority tier (for capacity planning)?
- Did a priority-heavy load starve default-priority requests?

### Proposed change

When `--scheduling-policy priority` is enabled, add a **bucketed `priority`
label** to every finished-request metric so Grafana/queries can break down
latency and throughput per priority tier:

| Request priority | `priority` label |
|---|---|
| `-1` / `0` / `1` | preserved exactly (high / default / low) |
| other integers | collapse into `<-1` / `>1` |

The three conventional values carry semantic meaning, so they are preserved
exactly; everything else is bucketed to **bound Prometheus cardinality to five
values** (raw integers would allow clients to blow up cardinality, e.g. with
deadline-based priorities).

Two new metrics:

- `vllm:request_priority` (Histogram): distribution of raw finished-request
  priorities. Registered only under priority scheduling, so FCFS output is
  unchanged.
- `vllm:scheduler_policy_info` (Gauge): enum-style indicator of the active
  scheduler policy (always exposed), so dashboards can discover which policy a
  deployment runs without scraping logs.

To label TTFT, its observation moves from iteration-level
(`IterationStats.time_to_first_tokens_iter`) to the finished-request context —
the per-request value is already tracked in `RequestStateStats.first_token_latency`,
so the measured value is identical.

FCFS output is byte-for-byte unchanged: no `priority` label, no new histogram,
the only addition is the always-on `scheduler_policy_info` gauge.

### Prior art / duplicate check

I searched open PRs/issues for priority metrics/observability and found nothing
addressing this. Related (but disjoint) work: scheduler behavior
(#47837, #45558, #54530, #44166), KV-transfer QoS (#46016). No PR adds a
priority dimension to request metrics.

### Ask

Would this design be acceptable? Specifically interested in maintainer
feedback on:
1. the five-value label bucketing (vs. some other cardinality bound),
2. exposing `scheduler_policy_info` unconditionally (vs. hidden-metrics
   gating).

I have a working implementation with unit tests and a real-server E2E
verification ready to submit as a PR once the approach gets a thumbs-up.

hits.title: [Bug]: P2P KV offload tier runs NIXL peer registration synchronously inside the scheduler step, stalling all requests on the rank
hits.body:
### Your current environment

vLLM main @ 042ab0305c, NIXL 1.4.1, OffloadingConnector with `secondary_tiers: [{"type": "p2p"}]`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When a P2P peer connects, the receiving rank registers it with NIXL **synchronously on the engine's scheduler thread, inside the scheduler step**. Until registration finishes, that rank cannot schedule its next batch. This hits **every request on the rank**, including running decodes that have nothing to do with P2P. It is a scheduling bug, separate from the P2P lookup latency in #55179.

Call path on main:

```
EngineCore.step()
  -> scheduler.schedule() -> OffloadingConnectorScheduler.build_connector_meta()
    -> TieringManager.on_schedule_end()
      -> P2P tier serve_external_requests() -> P2PSession.poll()
        -> P2PSession._on_connect()                    # p2p/session/session.py
          -> NixlTransport.add_remote_peer()           # p2p/data/nixl.py
               add_remote_agent(metadata)
               [one Python descriptor tuple per block]  # O(num_blocks)
               get_xfer_descs(...)
               prep_xfer_dlist(...)                     # O(num_blocks)
```

The cost grows linearly with the peer's CPU-tier block count (19,599 blocks per rank for a 64 GiB tier in #55179), and it is paid:

- on **both** peers, because each side handles the other's `ConnectMsg`;
- once per peer, so a rank in a DP×N mesh pays it N-1 times, and pays it again whenever a peer restarts or joins;
- at a time the rank doesn't control. A remote engine starting up causes a stall on every existing rank.

#55179 describes this only as one term in a remote P2P lookup's latency. It does not cover the local effect: a rank that is serving its own traffic gets an inter-token-latency spike for all its running requests whenever any peer connects.

### Expected behavior

Peer registration should never block the scheduler step. The NIXL connector already does this for its own handshakes (`_handshake_initiation_executor`, `_background_nixl_handshake`).

### Relationship to open PRs

- #58168 (manager control-plane thread) moves P2P servicing off the scheduler thread. But registration still runs inside `poll_tiers()` under the manager lock, so `schedule()` blocks on that lock whenever registration outlasts the current model step. That is always the case on an idle or lightly loaded rank. It reduces the stall but doesn't remove it.
- #57139 fixes it: it builds the peer handles in a single-worker executor with no lock held, publishes them atomically, and sends `ConnectAck` only after registration completes. The ack is the barrier that ensures no peer can fetch before it is registered.

### Suggested validation

On a rank serving steady decode traffic, connect a cold peer and measure:

1. the duration of that rank's scheduler step and ITL during the connect, compared with steady state;
2. the time `add_remote_peer` takes, as a function of `num_blocks`.

Compare main, #58168 and #57139.

---

hits.title: [RFC]: Adaptive prefill token budget based on scheduling pressure
hits.body:
### Motivation.

vLLM exposes `max_num_batched_tokens` (MBT) as a static scheduling configuration. For long-context workloads, however, we observe that the latency-optimal token budget depends on the current scheduling pressure.

Under low scheduling pressure, a large MBT can improve prefill execution efficiency and reduce end-to-end latency. As concurrent prefill and decode work increases, a smaller prefill budget can become preferable by limiting prefill interference with active decoding.

This means that no single static MBT is optimal across changing load regimes.

We investigated this behavior across multiple models, workloads, and NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 5090, A100, and H100), including kernel-level profiling with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute. Based on these observations, we developed Prefill-Pressure Adaptive Scheduling (P-PAS), a lightweight policy that adapts the amount of prefill work admitted by the scheduler.

Across the main load sweep, P-PAS reduced average end-to-end latency by 8.5% relative to fixed MBT 2k and by 11.3% relative to fixed MBT 16k.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15171

Implementation, benchmarks, raw results, and profiling traces:
https://github.com/TimoSaemann/ppas-vllm

### Proposed Change.

Add an optional adaptive prefill-budget policy to the V1 scheduler.

The evaluated P-PAS policy uses scheduler state that is already available.
Let:

- `N_p` be the number of running and waiting prefill requests
- `N_d` be the number of running decode requests
- `N_th` be a prefill-pressure threshold
- `B_max` be the normal prefill token budget
- `B_cap` be the reduced prefill token budget

The policy is:

```text
if N_p >= N_th and N_d > 0:
    prefill_budget = B_cap
else:
    prefill_budget = B_max
```

For the experiments in the paper:

```text
N_th  = 2
B_max = 16384
B_cap = 2048
```

The global scheduler token budget remains unchanged. The adaptive budget only limits the aggregate amount of prefill work admitted within a scheduler iteration.

The current implementation is a small modification of the vLLM V1 scheduler and can be enabled or disabled without changing the standard scheduling behavior when disabled.

I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and make the policy/configuration interface consistent with the maintainers' preferred design.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

A working implementation for vLLM 0.22.1 is available in the repository linked above. If there is interest in this direction, I would be happy to adapt the implementation to the current vLLM scheduler and prepare a PR.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

hits.title: [RFC]: Adaptive throughput/latency profile for RL rollout long-tail
hits.body:
# [RFC]: Adaptive throughput/latency profile for RL rollout long-tail

## Motivation.

RL rollouts have two clearly distinguishable phases on the same engine:

- **Front phase (throughput-bound)**: trainer submits 256–1024 requests at once; batch is large, compute is saturated. MTP / spec decode is **negative-ROI** here — extra `propose() + verify()` FLOPs cost wall time without paying back.
- **Tail phase (latency-bound)**: 1–10 long-tail decodes remain; batch is tiny, memory bandwidth is idle. **This is exactly when spec decode pays off** — but today's vLLM forces a single static profile for the whole rollout.

The closest existing work:

- **#32374** [V1][Spec Decode] Add Dynamic SD — varies `K` (number of draft tokens) per *batch* based on offline-profiled goodput. Fits Full-CG and async scheduling. Already directionally endorsed by maintainers.
- **#36657** [RFC]: Dynamic Speculation Length with Confidence-Threshold Early Exit — adapts length per-step via drafter confidence; complementary technique.
- **#39359 / #40662** Synthetic Acceptance Rate — measurement infrastructure that lets dynamic-SD policies be evaluated without retraining drafters.
- **#25112** [Bug]: Spec decoding is not disabled at/after configured batch size — same problem statement; reports the deleted `disable_by_batch_size` (commit `aa08a30fc`, PR #35060).

This RFC proposes the **boundary case** of #32374: when a batch-level signal indicates compute saturation, set `K = 0` (skip `speculator.propose()` entirely) instead of just shrinking K. Same mechanism, same constraints, cleaner semantics for the `K=0` edge.

## Proposed Change.

### Scope (intentionally narrow)

1. **Batch-level only**, not per-request. (Per-request dynamism is explicitly out of scope; the complexity-vs-value tradeoff doesn't justify it before the proposer interface matures post-MRV2.)
2. **Async-scheduling-preserving**, no exceptions. No GPU→CPU sync added in the decision path. The detector reads CPU-side scheduler stats already available on every step.
3. **Reuse #32374's dispatch path** when it lands. The toggle proposed here is the `K=0` end of that spectrum; both should converge on the same `BatchDescriptor`-keyed Full-CG dispatch infrastructure that #32374 builds.

### Profile semantics

| Profile     | `speculator.propose()` | When                          |
|-------------|------------------------|-------------------------------|
| THROUGHPUT  | **skipped**            | Large batch, prefill-heavy    |
| LATENCY     | called                 | Long-tail decode, small batch |

### Three-level control

| Level | Mechanism                                                           | Trigger             | Use                                     |
|-------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| L0    | `RolloutPhaseDetector.observe()` in `EngineCore.step()`             | vLLM internal       | Default path                            |
| L1    | `collective_rpc("set_rollout_phase_override", profile)`             | Trainer (e.g. verl) | Pin during weight sync, debugging       |
| L2    | `compilation.adaptive_profile_enabled: bool = False`                | Startup config      | Off ⇒ today's static behavior           |

L1 takes precedence over L0; while overridden, the detector keeps observing but does not flip.

### Detector

Hook point: `vllm/v1/engine/core.py:391`, after `scheduler.schedule()` and before `execute_model`. Inputs are CPU-side fields already populated for the step: `len(scheduler.running)`, `len(scheduler.waiting)`, `scheduler_output.total_num_scheduled_tokens`. No GPU reads.

Default state machine (tunable):

```
THROUGHPUT (initial)
    │  for 5 consecutive steps:
    │    num_running / max_num_seqs < 0.20  AND
    │    median(scheduled_tokens / num_running over last 5) < 5.0
    ▼
  LATENCY
    │  for 3 consecutive steps:  num_running / max_num_seqs > 0.40
    │  OR num_waiting > 0  (incoming work ⇒ throughput immediately)
    ▼
THROUGHPUT
```

`wake_up()` resets the detector to THROUGHPUT (post-weight-update phases start fresh).

### Why this preserves async scheduling

1. KV cache and token budgets are demand-driven: `request.num_tokens_with_spec` collapses to `num_tokens` when `spec_token_ids` is empty.
2. In async mode, draft tokens flow via `_copy_draft_token_ids_to_cpu()` → `update_async_spec_token_ids()` directly into `sampling_metadata.spec_token_ids` for the rejection sampler — **not through `request.spec_token_ids`**.
3. `AsyncScheduler._update_after_schedule()` uses `[-1]` placeholders, not budget commitments.
4. The only coupling is `num_output_placeholders += 1 + cur_num_spec_tokens`. After a LATENCY → THROUGHPUT flip, the next step still increments by `1 + K` (using already-scheduled stale spec tokens). This is **one step of placeholder over-count, self-correcting on the following step** — behavioral overshoot, not a correctness bug.
5. PRs `fafe76b4a` ("Zero-bubble async scheduling + spec decoding") and `711edaf0d` already established the contract this RFC operates within.

**No scheduler changes. No GPU sync. No per-request branching.**

### Implementation footprint (Stage 1)

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `vllm/config/compilation.py` | Add `adaptive_profile_enabled: bool = False` |
| `vllm/config/speculative.py` | In `__post_init__`, set `runtime_skip_supported` per method (mtp/eagle/eagle3/ngram = True; suffix = False conservatively) |
| `vllm/v1/engine/rollout_phase_detector.py` | **New file**: `RolloutPhaseDetector` |
| `vllm/v1/engine/core.py` | Construct detector; observe in `step()`; reset in `wake_up()`; expose `set_rollout_phase_override` RPC |
| `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` | Add `_spec_decode_runtime_enabled`; new RPC `set_optimization_profile`; guard at `:4209` |

DSV3.2 + MTP gets the full benefit immediately because its `enforce_eager=True` means no cudagraph dimension to handle. For non-V3.2 MTP models that want cudagraph adaptation, we defer to #32374's Full-CG infrastructure rather than building a parallel one.

### Deployment topology (context, not a vLLM change)

For users on whom Stage 1 doesn't yet land or who want stronger isolation, two purely-deployment patterns work today with zero vLLM changes:

- **Multi-instance + router** — separate throughput/latency pools on different GPUs; route by request type or rollout phase. Mature routers (SGLang router / Envoy) handle the routing.
- **Two co-located processes + sleep/wake** — independent vLLM processes on the same GPU set, only one awake at a time, swap at rollout step boundaries via `sleep(level=2)` / `wake_up()`. Each process has its own `CuMemAllocator`. Wake latency is dominated by weight H2D over PCIe; for `enforce_eager=True` models there is no cudagraph re-capture cost. Constraint: swap requires in-flight = 0, so this pattern handles step-boundary phase shifts but not within-step adaptation — that remains Stage 1's job.

These patterns are recipes, not proposals — they may be worth documenting in a follow-up but they are not part of this RFC's request to vLLM.

### Rollout

1. **Stage 1 (this RFC)** — Detector + override RPC + `propose()` skip. Five-file change. Zero memory delta. No scheduler changes. Useful immediately for DSV3.2 + MTP.
2. **Stage 2** — Converge the detector's `K=0 / K=K_max` decision onto the same `BatchDescriptor`-keyed Full-CG dispatch path that #32374 introduces, so dynamic SD with `K ∈ {0, …, K_max}` and the on/off toggle share infrastructure.
3. **Stage 3** — Metrics (`current_profile` gauge, flip counter), verl integration recipe (pin THROUGHPUT around weight updates).

### Open questions

1. Is the detector's hook point in `EngineCore.step()` acceptable, or would the SIG prefer it as a plugin / external scheduler hook?
2. Detector defaults (`0.20` enter / `0.40` exit / window 5 / debounce 5,3 / tokens-per-req threshold 5.0) — reasonable across model sizes, or per-model defaults?
3. `runtime_skip_supported` — defaulting to True for mtp/eagle/eagle3/ngram, False for suffix. Looking for sign-off from method maintainers.
4. Async overshoot at flip: 1 step of placeholder over-count is acceptable to us. Is that acceptable to the SIG, or is strict zero-overshoot required?
5. Stage-2 convergence with #32374: should this RFC wait for #32374 to land, or proceed with a temporary skip path that #32374 can later subsume?

### Verification

- **Unit**: synthetic step traces for the detector — assert hysteresis, `num_waiting > 0` short-circuit, override pinning, median window vs single-step outliers. No torch sync in the detector path (verified via `torch.cuda.set_sync_debug_mode`).
- **Integration**: DSV3.2 + MTP, submit 256 prompts (one with `max_tokens=8192`, rest ≤32). Assert (a) flip log around long-tail; (b) outputs bit-identical to non-adaptive baseline at the same seed; (c) tail-segment TTLT_p99 reduction. Re-run with `async_scheduling=True` for parity.
- **Benchmark**: H200, Pareto output-length workload, 4 arms (always-on / always-off / adaptive / static-router). Expect adaptive to match always-off on the head and always-on on the tail.

### Risks

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Detector flapping | 5-in / 3-out hysteresis; `num_waiting > 0` short-circuit; flip-count metric |
| Mis-flip during weight update | Trainer pins THROUGHPUT before `start_weight_update`; `wake_up` resets detector |
| 1-step async overshoot | Documented as acceptable; if not, observation point can move ahead of `schedule()` |
| Divergence from #32374 | Stage 2 explicitly converges on shared dispatch infrastructure |

### Out of scope

- Per-request profile dynamism.
- Speculator unload/reload (MTP heads are part of the model weight set).
- A `cuda_graph` tag for sleep/wake (would help the deployment-topology recipes; separate RFC).

## Feedback Period.

Two weeks from posting.

## CC List.

@benchislett @LucasWilkinson @ekagra-ranjan @jmamou — flagging because this RFC is positioned as a boundary case of the dynamic-SD work in #32374 / #36657 / #39359 / #40662, and async-scheduling preservation is an explicit hard constraint shaped by your prior discussion. Happy to fold this into either of those threads if that's preferred over a separate RFC.

## Any Other Things.

- AI assistance was used in drafting. The submitter understands every claim and code path referenced and will defend the design end-to-end.
- Empirical numbers (DSV3.2 + MTP on H200) will be posted as a follow-up comment.

hits.title: [Bugfix] Fix pipeline load imbalance in scheduler
hits.body:
## Purpose
In the current pipeline parallel implementation (non-Ray V2), the scheduler allows the first stage to greedily schedule requests up to the global max_num_seqs limit. It does not account for the capacity of downstream pipeline stages. This leads to severe load imbalance where the first stage becomes a bottleneck, causing downstream stages to starve or forcing the pipeline to process requests in inefficient "stop-and-wait" bursts.
This PR fixes the imbalance by introducing a constraint on the number of requests scheduled in the "pre-pipeline" phase. We calculate a fair share of requests per pipeline stage (max_num_pre_pipeline_reqs) and enforce this limit during the scheduling of running, new, and resumed requests.

**Examples:**
1. Underutilization (Small Batch): With max_num_seqs=32 and pipeline_parallel_size=2, if a user sends 16 requests, the scheduler might try to push all 16 into the first stage. This leaves the second stage idle initially and creates a bursty workload. Ideally, the load should be balanced (8 requests per stage) to keep the pipeline full.
2. Since the pipeline speed is limited by the slowest stage, the stage with 18 requests becomes a straggler, increasing overall latency.

hits.title: [Observability] Add structured per-request context to preemption warnings
hits.body:
## Summary

Add a `logger.warning()` call inside `Scheduler._preempt_request()` that emits
structured per-request context at the exact moment a request is evicted from the
running queue due to KV cache exhaustion.

## Motivation

When preemption occurs under memory pressure, the current V1 runtime has:
- A cumulative Prometheus preemption counter
- A `PREEMPTED` lifecycle event recorded per request (for latency metrics)
- `preempted_req_ids` in `SchedulerOutput`

None of these produce a human-readable log entry at the preemption site with
context useful for diagnosing the root cause. Operators observing latency spikes
from preemption thrash (e.g. #25538, closed not_planned) currently have no way
to identify which request was evicted, how much computed work was discarded, or
what memory pressure looked like at the moment it happened.

## What this PR adds

A single `logger.warning()` in `_preempt_request()`, capturing:

- `request_id` — which request was evicted
- `num_computed_tokens` lost — recompute cost on resume (captured before `free()`)
- `kv_cache_usage` before → after — memory pressure context
- per-request `num_preemptions` — identifies thrash on a single long request

Example output:
```
WARNING [scheduler.py] Preempting request cmpl-abc123: 480 computed tokens lost
(recompute on resume), kv_cache_usage 98.4% -> 96.1%. Preemption count for this
request: 1. To reduce preemptions, increase gpu_memory_utilization or
max_model_len, or decrease max_num_seqs.
```

## Relation to #36449

This PR is not a duplicate of #36449 ("[Observability] Add scheduler preemption
metrics"). That PR adds aggregate metrics and summary-level log visibility.
This PR adds per-event structured context at the preemption call site itself —
complementary, not overlapping. Both can merge independently.

## Changes

- `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`: capture `num_computed_tokens` and
  `kv_cache_manager.usage` before `free()`, emit `logger.warning()` after.
  No behavior changes. Existing counters and events are unchanged.
- `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py`: two new tests using the existing
  `create_scheduler` / `create_requests` / `ModelRunnerOutput` harness.
  Forces KV exhaustion to trigger preemption, asserts warning is emitted with
  expected structured fields. No GPU required.

hits.title: [Perf][DeepSeek-V3] Dynamic MLA/MHA Routing for Sub-1024 Token Prefill (~3x TTFT Speedup)
hits.body:
Description:
Problem:
vLLM currently routes all DeepSeek-V3 MLA prefills through the "absorbed" pathway. While memory-optimal for long contexts, this path is computationally inefficient for short-context prefills, resulting in a 3.36x FLOP overhead.

Solution:
Implemented MLAPathSelector to dynamically branch attention routing:

Threshold: < 1024 tokens.

Action: Routes to un-absorbed MHA, bypassing ops.concat_and_cache_mla() and reducing mathematical prefill cost by ~70%.

Fallback: Sequences > 1024 tokens maintain the original absorbed logic to ensure VRAM stability and retrieval accuracy.

Impact:

Projected ~65% reduction in TTFT for common 512-token chat/instruction prompts.

Backend-agnostic (FlashInfer/Triton).

Zero-overhead routing integrated into the Forward pass.

Closes #31473

hits.title: [Bugfix][MoE] Keep routing rows during DeepSeek V4.1 decoder replay
hits.body:
## Overview

Keep every prefill routing row when DeepSeek V4.1 decoder replay runs with returned routed experts enabled. Extracted from #61388 as a standalone fix based on `main`.

## Claims

- R3 requests use the existing prompt-logprobs keep-row mechanism so decoder replay does not omit their routing computations.
- Cover eager and PIECEWISE replay in the existing replay-batch suite.
- The diff contains the request row-retention policy and its regression coverage in two files.

## Validation

- **20 isolated CPU policy cases passed** using the actual request-admission, graph-selection, and replay row-selection methods with real CPU tensors. The same checks against unmodified `main` reproduce **6 failures / 14 passes**, including a 300-row prefill incorrectly reduced to 128 rows.
- Applicable pre-commit hooks, including mypy and Buildkite test tethering, and `git diff --check`: passed with local UTF-8/Git Bash interpreter adaptations.
- The pre-split #61388 validation recorded real-weight DeepSeek-V4.1 TP1/DP2/EP, 300/301-token prefill: late layers previously executed only 128 rows; the keep-row fix retained all rows in all 40 layers. The request-retention change is preserved from that combined revision.

GPU/model runs were not repeated for the split. CPU checks stop at the row-selection boundary and substitute configuration/base-state/input-gather fixtures; they do not validate CUDA kernels or attention numerics. The GPU regression remains in the existing CI-tethered suite:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/models/test_deepseek_v41_replay_batch.py
```

## Details

Decoder replay can normally skip older prefill rows when only final logits are needed. Returned routing needs every accepted token's decisions; scattering the remaining rows cannot recover computations that never ran. Mark R3 requests as requiring every row when admitted, using the existing keep-row policy.

R3-enabled replay therefore retains prefill work that could otherwise be trimmed. No throughput measurement is claimed.

Duplicate-work checks refreshed open PR searches for `61388 in:body`, routed-expert capture, and decoder replay. #52902 adds API consistency tests, #57184 handles DBO staging/offsets, and #56778 implements terminal transport; they do not implement this NVIDIA V4.1 admission policy. The same fix has been removed from #61388, so this is its single review location.

AI assistance was used to split and validate the existing fix.

hits.title: [Bugfix][SM120][MLA] Disable dense prefill for FlashInfer sparse MLA
hits.body:
## Purpose

Fix long-prompt prefill failures in `FlashInferMLASparseSM120Impl`.

The SM120 sparse backend inherits `supports_dense_mha_prefill = True` from `MLAAttentionImpl`, but it implements only the sparse `forward_mqa` path. When a long prompt selects dense or masked MHA prefill, the shared MLA router accesses dense-path state such as `masked_mha_available`, which this implementation does not define.

This change overrides the inherited capability with `supports_dense_mha_prefill = False`. The existing MLA routing then leaves `prefill_backend` unset and sends all prefill tokens through the supported sparse-MQA path. Other MLA implementations and decode routing are unchanged.

A backend API regression test verifies that the SM120 implementation remains sparse and does not advertise dense-MHA prefill support.

### Duplicate-work check

No open PR or issue was found for `supports_dense_mha_prefill`, `masked_mha_available`, or this SM120 prefill failure. PR #46994 also touches this class, but only changes MTP top-k buffer handling and does not modify prefill capabilities or routing.

### AI assistance disclosure

hits.title: [ROCm][MoRIIO] Fix WRITE prefill-block release routing under Wide-EP
hits.body:
## Purpose

`MoRIIOConnectorScheduler._release_write_prefill_blocks` frees the producer's
deferred KV blocks when a request finishes with `do_remote_prefill` still set —
i.e. it was aborted before `update_state_after_alloc` ever ran.

It addressed the producer with the **raw global** `remote_dp_rank` and
`remote_host`:

```python
target_port = remote_notify_port + get_port_offset(remote_dp_rank, tp_index)
self._send_transfer_release(transfer_id, remote_host, target_port)
```

The notify path in `update_state_after_alloc` resolves the same destination
differently — it folds the rank to its pod-local value and looks up the owning
pod's host:

```python
_remote_dp_rank_for_port = fold_local_rank(remote_dp_rank, _dp_local)
_pod_idx = pod_index(remote_dp_rank, _dp_local)
_notify_host = _remote_hosts[_pod_idx]
```

Under multi-pod Wide-EP the two disagree for every rank on a child pod. At
DP=16 / `dp_local=8`, half the ranks are misrouted:

| rank | notify (correct) | release (before) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–7 | `10.0.0.10:61005`–`61012` | same — match |
| 8 | `10.0.0.11:61005` | `10.0.0.10:61013` |
| 12 | `10.0.0.11:61009` | `10.0.0.10:61017` |
| 15 | `10.0.0.11:61012` | `10.0.0.10:61020` |

A pod binds notify sockets only for its **local** ranks, so both pods listen on
`61005`–`61012`. The release for ranks 8–15 targets `61013`–`61020`, which
nothing binds — so it is **dropped**, not misdelivered. Since this release is
the only thing that frees those blocks (no timeout, no GC, no retry), each
occurrence strands one request's worth of prefill KV for the lifetime of the
process, silently.

Single-pod deployments are unaffected: the modulus is a no-op and there is one
host, so both paths already agreed.

## Why it went unnoticed

`_release_write_prefill_blocks` predates multi-pod support. `fold_local_rank`
and `pod_index` were introduced later, when Wide-EP multi-pod landed, and
applied to the notify path. The release function was pre-existing code that had
always been correct, and nothing in it flagged that its assumptions had changed.

It is also hard to hit in testing: the trigger is an abort *before* scheduling,
so a benchmark where every request completes never executes the path at all.

## Changes

- Reuse the notify path's per-pod resolution in the release path. Both helpers
  were already imported.
- Raise the two early-return guards from `warning` to `error` and include the
  transfer id and DP rank. Each of those returns leaks blocks with no other
  reclaim path, so the leak should at least be attributable. (Deliberately not
  converted to exceptions — that would change behaviour in a path that
  currently degrades gracefully.)

## Test Plan

New: `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_moriio_write_release_routing.py`

Follows `test_moriio_routing.py`'s convention of binding the unbound method to
a lightweight stand-in. Covers:

- master-pod ranks (0–7) unchanged; child-pod ranks (8–15) reach the owning pod
  at the folded offset
- the property directly: for all 16 ranks, release target == notify target
- every release lands on a port a pod actually binds
- single-pod and the `dp_local == 0` external-DP sentinel are byte-identical to
  before the change
- degenerate inputs: missing `remote_hosts`, host list shorter than the pod
  index, non-numeric `dp_local`
- TP fan-out at `tp_size=2`
- both leak guards: nothing sent, error logged naming the request, transfer id
  and rank

## Test Result

Run inside a ROCm vLLM image on an MI355X node.

Against the **unpatched** connector, the suite fails exactly where expected:

```
22 failed, 29 passed
```

The 22 failures are the child-pod ranks, their bound-port assertions, the
all-16-rank parity property, TP fan-out, and the two guards. The 29 passes are
the master-pod ranks, single-pod and the sentinel — the cases that should not
be affected.

With the fix applied:

```
97 passed
```

Full MoRIIO suite, no regressions:

```
159 passed, 25 skipped in 80.23s
```

hits.title: [Kernel] SM120: stop routing misaligned-M blockwise FP8 GEMMs to the small-M swapAB config
hits.body:
## Purpose

The SM120 blockwise FP8 GEMM dispatch routes **every** call with `M % 4 != 0` to the
swapAB config (TILE_N=32), which was added in #38325 as a small-M/decode optimization:

```cpp
bool swap_ab = (M <= 64) || (M % 4 != 0);
```

Under V1 chunked prefill, mixed prefill+decode batches routinely make M misaligned at
prefill scale (M ~ 8k). In an Nsight Systems capture of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (a dense 27B
hybrid linear-attention model: 64 layers, 3:1 gated-delta-net to full attention, FP8
e4m3 blockwise) serving 8192/1024-token requests at concurrency 32 on an NVIDIA RTX PRO
6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120), 82% of prefill-scale blockwise GEMM
instances (14400/17523) went through the swapAB path, where they averaged 4.84 ms vs
3.10 ms on the default 128x128x128 config. The misroute roughly doubled prefill GEMM
time end-to-end.

Force-routing both paths over a dense M x N x alignment matrix (M = 48..8192 including
M%4 in {0,1,2}, N in {5120, 15360, 34816}, K = 5120) shows:

- swapAB only wins at M <= ~80 (its intended decode regime);
- from M ~ 96-128 up, the non-swap configs win everywhere, by 1.3x-2.0x at prefill scale;
- outputs are **bit-identical** between the swapAB and non-swap paths at every measured
  misaligned point, so the `M % 4 != 0` clause has no correctness role on SM120.

The fix restricts swapAB to its design regime:

```cpp
bool swap_ab = (M <= 64);
```

Note: `scaled_mm_blockwise_sm90_fp8_dispatch.cuh` (`(a.size(0) % 4) != 0`) and
`scaled_mm_blockwise_sm100_fp8_dispatch.cuh` (`(m < 16) || (m % 4 != 0)`) carry the same
misaligned-M clause. They are untouched here because the measurements above are
SM120-only; the same recheck may be worthwhile on those targets.

## Test Plan

- Microbenchmark driving `torch.ops._C.cutlass_scaled_mm` across an M x N x alignment
  matrix with both kernel paths force-routed (temporary env-var instrumentation, not
  included in this PR), comparing per-path latency and bitwise outputs.
- End-to-end serving benchmark before/after: 8192-token prompts, 1024-token outputs,
  concurrency 32, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, Qwen3.8-27B-FP8.

## Test Result

Microbenchmark (N=34816, K=5120):

| M | before (ms) | after (ms) |
|---|---|---|
| 64 | 0.13 | 0.13 (unchanged, still swapAB) |
| 8192 (M%4==0) | 3.86 | 3.89 (unchanged) |
| 8193 | 7.89 | 4.12 |
| 8225 | 7.64 | 3.92 |

Outputs at M=8193/8225 are bit-identical before and after.

End-to-end (concurrency 32, 8K/1K):

| metric | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| output throughput | 424.6 tok/s | 499.8 tok/s (+17.7%) |
| mean TTFT | 9660 ms | 6872 ms |
| mean TPOT | 65.9 ms | 57.3 ms |

The patched build reaches parity with an SGLang baseline of the same model, shapes, and
hardware (501.2 tok/s), closing what was previously an ~18% gap that traced back to this
misroute.

hits.title: [Model] Optimize Sarvam MLA routing and preserve FP32 router logits
hits.body:
## Purpose

Fix Sarvam MLA's missing flat-routing configuration and preserve the configured router-logit dtype through expert selection. On the tested BF16 B200 setup, these changes enable the supported TRTLLM MoE path and reduce router overhead while removing an unnecessary BF16 narrowing of FP32 logits.

The source diff is confined to `vllm/model_executor/models/sarvam.py`:

- Default absent or `None` `n_group` and `topk_group` to `1`. The model uses flat top-8-of-128 routing (verified). A single group expresses that configuration and allows the supported TRTLLM implementation to be selected. Explicit checkpoint values are preserved.
- Replace `nn.Linear` plus input/output casts with the existing `GateLinear(out_dtype=router_dtype)`. With the default FP32 router output, the tested path uses BF16 inputs/weights and FP32 accumulation/output, and keeps those logits in FP32 for routing. Previously, the FP32 linear result was narrowed to the hidden-state dtype before expert selection. Other configured router output dtypes remain respected.

### Duplicate-work check

Searched open upstream PRs for `sarvam`, `sarvam routing`, and `sarvam GateLinear`; no open PR addressing these router changes was found.

## Test Plan

Validation below combines local checks on the merged branch with historical GPU experiments on the constituent changes. **The GPU results predate the latest upstream merge; they are not a fresh evaluation of this merged head.** This is a draft for human review and post-merge validation.

### Performance

Plain Sarvam step-1350 checkpoint, BF16, 2× NVIDIA B200, TP=2, no speculative model. Gate comparisons used EP off, compilation enabled, prefix caching disabled, maximum model length 32,768, and fixed real-data prompts truncated to 8,192 tokens. Each case used five timing repetitions and medians. Decode step time was estimated as `(median time for 136 output tokens − median time for 8 output tokens) / 128`, with EOS ignored. Prefill throughput uses the corresponding timing intercept and includes admission/scheduler overhead.


| Batch | Control decode ms/step | Repeated control | GateLinear decode ms/step | Speedup against both controls |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4.844 | 4.664 | 4.473 | 1.043–1.083× |
| 32 | 15.806 | 15.747 | 15.304 | 1.029–1.033× |

| Batch | Control prefill tokens/s | Repeated control | GateLinear prefill tokens/s | Speedup against both controls |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 62,419 | 62,298 | 67,078 | 1.075–1.077× |
| 32 | 67,655 | 67,035 | 70,294 | 1.039–1.049× |

Separately, the flat-routing defaults switched the tested MoE path from CUTLASS to TRTLLM and measured **1.11–1.17× decode throughput and 1.03–1.04× prefill throughput**.

### Routing precision verification

An isolated router experiment used real gate weights from all 31 MoE layers, synthetic layer-normalization-scaled inputs, 65,536 inputs per layer, and three seeds on B200: **6,094,848 layer/input comparisons**.

| Candidate compared with the old FP32-gate → BF16-logit path | Inputs with a different selected expert set |
| --- | ---: |
| BF16 gate, still narrow logits to BF16 | 630 / 6,094,848 (0.0103%) |
| BF16 gate, retain FP32 logits | 133,833 / 6,094,848 (2.1958%) |
| FP32 gate, retain FP32 logits | 133,842 / 6,094,848 (2.1960%) |

Removing the logit downcast accounts for the dominant change in expert selection. This is intentionally not bit-exact to the old path: rounding logits before sigmoid/bias/top-k can alter close routing decisions. These counts measure expert-set disagreement, not task error rates, and do not establish exact equivalence between the two FP32-output candidates or full training/inference numerical parity.
Separate evals like AIME, GPQA, TAU2, etc were conducted to ensure parity in quality.

### End-to-end repeatability

Each run scored the same **687,500 positions across 200 fixed prompts**, up to 4,096 tokens each, at **concurrency 1**, with 2×B200, TP=2, EP enabled, BF16, compilation enabled, and prefix caching disabled. A disagreement means a different top-1 next token given the same dataset prefix; this is teacher-forced agreement, not diverging free-running generations. Captures contain top-1 token IDs and saved log probabilities, not full logit tensors.

| Historical build | Selected MoE backend | Top-1 differences against its repeat |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Base commit (main) | CUTLASS | 67,408 / 687,500 (9.805%) |
| Flat-routing defaults (`879e62199d`) | TRTLLM | 0; saved log probabilities bit-identical |
| GateLinear / FP32 logits (`647516fb80`) | TRTLLM | 0; saved log probabilities bit-identical |

Each repeat pair shared an allocation; different historical builds ran on different nodes using the dependencies installed at experiment time. The measured repeatability boundary is the flat-routing/backend-selection change. This does not isolate the internal cause of the earlier variance or establish determinism at higher concurrency.

Cross-implementation diagnostics also showed that scale placement and bias handling affect Sarvam-versus-DeepSeek agreement. Those diagnostic modifications are excluded from this PR; DeepSeek agreement is not treated as proof of task accuracy.

## Test Result

Checks run on the merged branch:

```text
uv tool run ruff check vllm/model_executor/models/sarvam.py        PASS
uv tool run ruff format --check vllm/model_executor/models/sarvam.py  PASS
git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD                           PASS
```

AI assistance was used to prepare and review this contribution and summarize the recorded experiments. Human review and final validation remain required.

hits.title: [Bugfix][Spec-Decode] TurboQuant K+1 spec-verify routing (fixes #40880)
hits.body:
## Summary

Fixes #40880 (degenerate token cascade on Qwen3.6-MoE under MTP=3 + FULL_AND_PIECEWISE cudagraph + TurboQuant k8v4 KV cache).

Adds a dispatch branch in `TurboQuantAttentionImpl.forward()` that detects uniform K+1 spec-verify batches and routes them through `triton_turboquant_decode_attention` via the `synth_seq_lens` trick (same pattern `_continuation_prefill` uses internally). Restores `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` cudagraph for spec-decode while fixing the correctness bug.

## Root cause

When speculative decoding (`num_speculative_tokens=K>0`) is active, the verify pass produces **uniform-query batches** with `max_query_len = K+1` (e.g., MTP K=3 → q_len=4 per request) where `max_seq_len > max_query_len` (each request has prior cached KV).

The default `_prefill_attention` continuation branch reads `query_start_loc.tolist()` which:
1. Forces a GPU→CPU sync incompatible with active CUDA stream capture
2. When paired with the spec-verify pattern, computes attention to ONLY the current chunk's K/V (ignoring prior cached KV)

Drafter and verifier converge on the same high-bias special token (e.g. `<tool_call>`) → cascade output. Reproducer well-documented in #40880 with multi-rig confirmation.

## Existing workarounds in the wild

These all work but trade off correctness vs throughput:

- **Surgical capture-guard** via `is_current_stream_capturing()` check (e.g. [@noonghunna's `patch_tolist_cudagraph.py`](https://github.com/noonghunna/qwen36-27b-single-3090/blob/master/patches/patch_tolist_cudagraph.py))
- **`cudagraph_mode=NONE`** — disables FULL CG entirely, ~30% TPS cost
- **PIECEWISE downgrade** for spec-decode — Genesis project's P65 workaround

This PR replaces all three with a proper architectural fix.

## Fix design

```python
# In TurboQuantAttentionImpl.forward(), BEFORE the existing dispatch:

_spec_verify_eligible = (
    attn_metadata.is_prefill
    and num_decodes == 0
    and 1 < attn_metadata.max_query_len <= 16
    and attn_metadata.max_seq_len > attn_metadata.max_query_len
    and N > 0
    and (N % attn_metadata.max_query_len) == 0
    and attn_metadata.query_start_loc is not None
)
if _spec_verify_eligible:
    # Build synth args mirroring _continuation_prefill's pattern (all GPU ops):
    #   synth_seq_lens[req*K1+i] = base_seq_lens[req] - K1 + 1 + i
    #   synth_block_table[req*K1+i] = block_table[req]
    # Then route through `triton_turboquant_decode_attention`.
```

The decode kernel:
- Handles compressed K+V cache lookup natively (no `.tolist()` needed)
- Has no CPU sync — fully cudagraph-safe
- Already proven correct on the spec-decode K+1 verify path via `_continuation_prefill`'s internal use

## Empirical results

| Config | TPS | Tool-call clean rate |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (P65 PIECEWISE downgrade workaround) | 57.2 tok/s | (pre-fix: cascades) |
| **This PR** | **75.6 tok/s** | **18/18 PASS** |
| | **+32% wall-clock** | (no cascades on the same reproducer) |

Hardware: 2× RTX A5000 (Ampere SM 8.6), TP=2, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8, MTP num_speculative_tokens=3, TurboQuant k8v4 KV cache.

Reproducer + full benchmark scripts: https://github.com/Sandermage/genesis-vllm-patches (v7.42-v7.44).

## Cross-arch validation

⚠️ **Tested ONLY on NVIDIA Ampere SM 8.6** (RTX A5000 primary, RTX 3090 cross-rig confirmation by @noonghunna).

**Hopper / Blackwell not yet tested.** Validators with that hardware would be very welcome — the routing path is architecturally agnostic (`triton_turboquant_decode_attention` already runs on all CUDA arches), but I can't claim cross-arch correctness without empirical data.

## Tests

`tests/v1/attention/test_turboquant_spec_verify.py`:
- `test_synth_seq_lens_shape` — verifies the `(B*K_PLUS_1,)` reshape produces the expected per-request pattern
- `test_synth_dtypes_preserved` — int32/int64 dtype preservation
- `test_synth_construction_no_cpu_sync` — runs synth construction inside `torch.cuda.graph()` capture (the property that makes routing safe)
- `test_eligibility_predicate` — eligibility checks for K+1=4, K+1=1 (decode), no-prior-cache, oversized K+1

End-to-end correctness test (requires a Qwen3.6 / TurboQuant model checkpoint) deferred to maintainer integration CI.

## Companion patches in our project (not in this PR)

For context, our public repo ships an alternative custom Triton kernel approach (`P67/P67b` in https://github.com/Sandermage/genesis-vllm-patches) which delivered the same 75.6 tok/s. This PR uses the **conservative routing-only approach** (no new kernel code) because it minimizes the diff and reuses upstream's proven decode kernel. Either is functionally equivalent for the bug fix.

## Stakeholders / for awareness

- @noonghunna — reported #40880, multi-rig confirmation. Their `patch_tolist_cudagraph.py` was the first capture-guard prototype in the wild.
- @vibhavagarwal5 — TurboQuant backend author (#38479). Would value review for any TQ-side change.
- @mgoin — recent TurboQuant routing fix (#40060). Quick technical feedback would help.
- @huangzhilin-hzl — TurboQuant FA3/FA4 prefill (#40092). For awareness — this PR touches an adjacent code path.

## Test plan

- [x] Boot test on Ampere SM 8.6 (RTX A5000, TP=2)
- [x] Tool-call regression (18/18 clean on `<tool_call>` cascade reproducer from #40880)
- [x] Bench (+32% TPS verified)
- [x] Long-context smoke (252K tokens, no regression)
- [ ] Cross-arch validation on Hopper / Blackwell (need help)
- [ ] Maintainer integration CI green

hits.body:
## Purpose
This PR aims to enable batch invariance for hybrid mamba models like Nemotron 3 or Bamba. The mamba layers don't prevent models from passing the existing "bs1_vs_bsN" tests, but batch invariance breaks down as soon as chunked prefill or prefix caching come into play - scenarios not verified by the current tests. To fix this, this PR does two things when in batch-invariant mode:

- force chunked prefill to split prompts only at mamba chunk boundaries
- align prefix cache entries to mamba chunk boundaries

It does not affect behavior in the default, non-batch-invariant mode.

## Test Plan
Added new tests to verify those scenarios:

```
$ VLLM_TEST_MODEL="ibm-ai-platform/Bamba-9B-v2" pytest tests/v1/determinism/test_prefix_caching_batch_invariance.py
$ VLLM_TEST_MODEL="ibm-ai-platform/Bamba-9B-v2" pytest tests/v1/determinism/test_chunked_prefill_batch_invariance.py

hits.body:
## Summary

`_random_prompt(min_words, max_words)` in `tests/v1/determinism/utils.py` silently produced prompts ~5× shorter than requested: it padded with `target_words // 50` repetitions of a 9-word filler instead of honoring the requested word count (a leftover `TODO` already flagged the discrepancy). Every prompt-length assumption in the determinism suite was therefore dishonest — e.g. "very long" `(1536, 3072)`-word prompts actually came out to only ~250–450 tokens.

This PR:

1. Fixes `_random_prompt` so it actually reaches `target_words` words.
2. Re-tunes the two callers that depended on the buggy lengths:
   - `test_v1_generation_is_deterministic_across_batch_sizes_with_needle`: `VLLM_MIN_PROMPT`/`VLLM_MAX_PROMPT` defaults 1024/2048 → 256/512, keeping the needle within a bounded KV-cache window for a 128-sequence batch (~1.5 tokens/word).
   - `test_logprobs_bitwise_batch_invariance_bs1_vs_bsN`: enables `enable_chunked_prefill=True` + `max_num_batched_tokens=2048`, and replaces the uniform 32×`(10,50)` prompts with ragged lengths (28×`(10,50)`, 50×`(256,512)`, 50×`(1000,1200)`) so the batched run exceeds the chunk threshold and actually exercises chunked prefill, while each prompt alone stays below it.

## Why this is not duplicating an existing PR

- No open PR touches `_random_prompt`; the only PRs referencing it are closed (#27054, #32480, #27421) and none fix the length bug.
- #46592 ("Feat/invariant with prefix cache") targets prefix-caching invariance, a separate and currently-broken feature; this PR does not enable prefix caching.
- #43317 ("Use token-id prefix in batch-invariant decode/prefill consistency test") fixes `test_decode_logprobs_match_prefill_logprobs`; this PR does not modify that test.
- #27054 (closed) stabilized the inverse `should_fail` test; this PR changes the shared prompt helper and the needle/chunked-prefill tests instead.

## Test plan

Machine: NVIDIA H20, `VLLM_TEST_MODEL=/data/models/Qwen3-1.7B`.

```
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py -v

- `test_logprobs_bitwise_batch_invariance_bs1_vs_bsN` — 6 passed (FLASH_ATTN/TRITON_ATTN/FLEX_ATTENTION × block_m 16/8)
- `test_simple_generation` — 3 passed
- `test_logprobs_without_batch_invariance_should_fail` — 3 passed
- `test_decode_logprobs_match_prefill_logprobs` — 1 passed

The full file is also exercised in CI (`.buildkite/test_areas/misc.yaml`) on A100/H100/B200.
