hits.title: Revert "[Mamba] enable prefix cache by default" (#50991)
hits.body:
## Purpose

Auto-revert of https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50991 ("[Mamba] enable prefix cache by default", commit `f9c74b4`).

Nightly CI build [#82382](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/82382) (commit `05b7876`) has **3 newly failing jobs** that all trace to this PR. All three passed at the previous analyzed nightly (#82083).

## Failures linked to this PR

| Job | Failure |
|---|---|
| `Language Models Test (PPL)` | `test_qwen.py::test_ppl[model_info2]` (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B`) — `ValidationError: Chunked prefill is required for mamba cache mode 'align'` |
| `Quantization` | `test_experts_int8.py::test_model_experts_int8_startup[4-bfloat16-ai21labs/Jamba-tiny-random]` — same `ValidationError` |
| `Extract Hidden States Integration` | `test_extract_hidden_states_qwen35_hybrid_smoke` — `AssertionError: Each KV cache group's real block_size must be divisible by hash_block_size. block_sizes=[544, 544, 544, 544, 181], hash_block_size=98464` in `HybridKVCacheCoordinator.__init__` |

## Root cause

The PR removed the `and not model_config.is_hybrid` guard in
`_set_default_chunked_prefill_and_prefix_caching_args` (`vllm/engine/arg_utils.py`), so prefix caching now
defaults to **on** for hybrid/Mamba models, and `vllm/model_executor/models/config.py` now unconditionally
defaults `mamba_cache_mode` to `"align"` instead of `"all"`.

Two consequences:

1. `"align"` mode asserts `scheduler_config.enable_chunked_prefill`. Any hybrid-model configuration that
   explicitly passes `enable_chunked_prefill=False` — previously valid, since prefix caching was off — now
   fails hard at `VllmConfig` validation. This is user-facing, not test-only: the two failing jobs above
   simply exercise that configuration. Logs confirm the new default firing:
   `config.py:599 Mamba cache mode is set to 'align' for Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration by default when prefix caching is enabled`.
2. Turning prefix caching on by default routes hybrid models through `HybridKVCacheCoordinator`, which then
   trips its own block-size divisibility assertion — a pre-existing defect that was unreachable while the
   feature stayed opt-in.

The PR updated `tests/models/language/generation/test_hybrid.py` to pass `enable_chunked_prefill=True`, but
other suites and real user configs were not covered.

Reverting restores the opt-in default. It touches only the 4 files the original PR touched and is an exact
inverse of `f9c74b4` (no conflicts, no manual resolution).

Opened as a **draft** so the author can instead land a forward fix if preferred.

<details>
<summary>Environment (excerpts)</summary>

- vLLM: **v0.20.0** (latest at time of report, Docker `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.20.0`)
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct-FP8`
- GPU: 1× NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada (48 GB)
- Driver / CUDA: as shipped in the v0.20.0 image

Launch flags (relevant):
\`\`\`
--model Qwen/Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct-FP8
--quantization fp8 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3
--max-model-len 8192
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.50
--enable-prefix-caching          # default
--enable-chunked-prefill         # default
--max-num-seqs 40
--seed 0
\`\`\`
</details>

### Describe the bug

\`Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration._get_deepstack_input_embeds\` raises \`ValueError\`, EngineCore catches it as fatal, and the engine dies (V1 \`EngineDeadError\`):

\`\`\`
File \"/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_vl.py\",
     line ~1716, in _get_deepstack_input_embeds
    raise ValueError(
ValueError: Requested more deepstack tokens than available in buffer:
            num_tokens=16 > self.deepstack_input_embeds_num_tokens=9
\`\`\`

The \`num_tokens\` requested is consistently **16** but the buffer's \`deepstack_input_embeds_num_tokens\` varies (we have observed **9, 11, 14**). EngineCore logs \`EngineCore encountered a fatal error\` → systemd has restarted the service **39 times in 3 days**.

### Reproduction signal

- **Workload:** OpenAI Chat Completions, single-image multimodal requests with prompts of 1500–2000 tokens. Production safety-monitoring pipeline that issues two-pass calls (primary + a longer \"rescue\" prompt on the same image).
- **First crash always happens after the engine has been serving normally for many minutes** — it isn't a startup issue.
- **Different \`mm_hash\` and different image content each crash** — this rules out a poison input being retried.
- **\`num_tokens=16\` is constant across all crashes** (Qwen3-VL deepstack always seems to request 16-token writes); the buffer size is whatever \`_set_deepstack_input_embeds\` wrote on the previous chunk.
- Prefix-cache hit count at crash time is high relative to prompt length (e.g. 1648/1657 hits → residual 9 tokens, which equals the \`_num_tokens=9\` in the error).

The pattern strongly suggests a chunked-prefill / prefix-cache misalignment: when prefix caching leaves a small residual chunk that lands inside the image's vision-token region, the buffer is sized to the chunk remainder while the language model still asks for the full 16-token deepstack contribution.

### Code pointer

\`vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_vl.py\`, in \`Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration.forward\`:

\`\`\`python
if inputs_embeds is not None and get_pp_group().is_first_rank:
    deepstack_input_embeds = self._get_deepstack_input_embeds(
        inputs_embeds.size(0)        # called with TOTAL step token count
    )
...
self._clear_deepstack_input_embeds(inputs_embeds.size(0))
\`\`\`

\`_get_deepstack_input_embeds\` is called with \`inputs_embeds.size(0)\` (total step tokens), while \`_set_deepstack_input_embeds\` was called earlier with the **vision-token count for the chunk that ran the vision encoder**. Across chunks of a single multimodal request these two counts are not the same — text-only chunks of a chunked prefill, and decode steps that happen to fall into the same image's deepstack window, both seem to trip the assert.

### Frequency

\`\`\`
\$ journalctl -u syncai-vllm-vl --since '2026-04-29' \\
    | grep 'Requested more deepstack tokens' | wc -l
39
\`\`\`

The first occurrence in our logs is **2026-04-29 18:52** (vLLM 0.20.0 was released 2026-04-27, two days earlier). The bug has happened roughly every 2–4 hours since under organic production load.

### Workaround we're testing

Setting \`--enable-chunked-prefill False\` on the vLLM launch — the assumption is that without chunked prefill, the deepstack \`_set\` always sees the full vision-token count and the \`_get\` call's \`inputs_embeds.size(0)\` aligns with what was written. Will report back.

A \`--enable-prefix-caching False\` workaround should also avoid the bad code path but with a worse latency hit.

### Suggested investigation

The buffer + index scheme in \`_get_deepstack_input_embeds\` / \`_set_deepstack_input_embeds\` / \`_clear_deepstack_input_embeds\` assumes a single-shot call per request — it tracks \`deepstack_input_embeds_num_tokens\` as a scalar instance attribute. Under chunked prefill of a multimodal request, the SAME \`Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration\` instance handles multiple chunks of the same request (and concurrent requests), so this scalar is racy.

Either:
1. The \`_get\` call site needs to compute the vision-token slice for *this chunk only* (not pass \`inputs_embeds.size(0)\`), or
2. The buffer needs a per-request key (req_id), or
3. Chunked prefill needs to be disabled for vision-encoder-bearing steps of multimodal requests.

### Before submitting a new issue

- [x] I have searched for existing issues — closest matches are unrelated (#38257 OOM, #29778 image_embeds out-of-bounds, #31404 MM cache AssertionError).
- [x] Latest version (v0.20.0).

## Purpose

This PR adds an opt-in prefix-cache-aware routing path for V1 internal data-parallel load balancing.

When `--data-parallel-prefix-cache-lb` is enabled, the frontend DP load balancer computes vLLM-compatible prompt block hashes and uses local best-effort prefix ownership state to choose a DP rank. The default behavior is unchanged.

Key points:

- Disabled by default.
- Only supports internal/local DP load balancing.
- Does not implement cross-DP KV import or warmup.
- Does not report external KV hits.
- Reuses vLLM prefix cache block hash semantics for routing signatures.
- Passes the resolved `hash_block_size` from EngineCore back to the frontend.
- Requires `PYTHONHASHSEED` when enabled so routing hashes are deterministic across processes.
- Adds an internal scheduler branch-point hint for align-mode Mamba/GDN prefill splitting.
- The branch-point hint only affects prefill chunk boundaries, not token contents or sampling semantics.

hits.title: [Docs] Document engine-aware routing with vLLM Router for DP deployments
hits.body:
Add a section to data_parallel_deployment.md explaining how vLLM Router's --intra-node-data-parallel-size flag combined with the consistent_hash policy enables session-affinity routing to individual DP engines within a single endpoint, useful for conversational/agentic workloads that benefit from prefix-cache reuse.

Closes #58160




## Purpose

Fixes #58160

The `data_parallel_deployment.md` page documents three ways to load-balance
requests across DP ranks (Internal, Hybrid, External), but doesn't mention
that [vLLM Router](https://github.com/vllm-project/router) can route
requests to *individual* DP engines within a deployment via
`--intra-node-data-parallel-size N`, combined with the `consistent_hash`
policy for session-affinity routing.

This is particularly useful for conversational/agentic workloads, where
pinning a session's follow-up requests to the same DP engine lets that
engine reuse its prefix/KV cache instead of recomputing it each turn.

As noted in the issue, this capability doesn't cleanly fit the existing
Internal/Hybrid/External classification, since it's an external tool that
is topology-aware rather than treating each endpoint as opaque. This PR
adds a new section, "Engine-Aware Routing with vLLM Router," after the
External Load Balancing section, with an example that composes it with
Hybrid Load Balancing.


## Test Plan

This is a documentation-only change (no code paths affected). Validated with:

- `pre-commit run markdownlint-cli2 --files docs/serving/data_parallel_deployment.md`
- Manual review of the rendered Markdown, including verifying the
  `#hybrid-load-balancing` anchor link and all external links resolve
  correctly.

## Test Result

`markdownlint-cli2` passed with no errors or warnings on the modified file.

hits.title: [Perf][DeepSeek-V3] Dynamic MLA/MHA Routing for Sub-1024 Token Prefill (~3x TTFT Speedup)
hits.body:
Description:
Problem:
vLLM currently routes all DeepSeek-V3 MLA prefills through the "absorbed" pathway. While memory-optimal for long contexts, this path is computationally inefficient for short-context prefills, resulting in a 3.36x FLOP overhead.

Solution:
Implemented MLAPathSelector to dynamically branch attention routing:

Threshold: < 1024 tokens.

Action: Routes to un-absorbed MHA, bypassing ops.concat_and_cache_mla() and reducing mathematical prefill cost by ~70%.

Fallback: Sequences > 1024 tokens maintain the original absorbed logic to ensure VRAM stability and retrieval accuracy.

Impact:

Projected ~65% reduction in TTFT for common 512-token chat/instruction prompts.

Backend-agnostic (FlashInfer/Triton).

Zero-overhead routing integrated into the Forward pass.

Closes #31473

## Purpose

On triton_kernels 3.8, which every ROCm build ships since #50605, the MoE routing metadata is rebuilt in torch with an int64 stable `argsort` and a `scatter_add_` histogram, costing 31–178 µs per MoE layer per step on MI355X / MI325X.

- `make_routing_data` sorts the ids in their own dtype and reads per-expert counts off the sorted keys with `searchsorted` instead of an atomic histogram. This path runs under expert parallelism and in `UnfusedOAITritonExperts`, which DeepSeek-V4 uses whenever AITER's MXFP4 MoE does not apply — on gfx942 that includes `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`.

hits.title: [Scheduler] Balance async PP decode batches
hits.body:
## Purpose

Balance established decode batches automatically when Model Runner V2 uses asynchronous pipeline parallelism.

Async PP makes a request eligible again after `pipeline_parallel_size` scheduler steps. Prompt-completion timing can therefore create persistent, uneven cadence groups such as Q7/Q13/Q2/Q10. This change limits established decode requests selected in each step to:

```text
ceil(max_num_seqs / pipeline_parallel_size)
```

The limit applies to both `RUNNING` requests and established decode requests resumed from `WAITING`. Prefill, chunked prefill, and chunks that complete a prompt in the current step remain uncapped because mixed batches require token-aware rather than sequence-count balancing. If priority preemption removes a selected decode, its cohort slot is restored.

The policy is active only for MRV2 `AsyncScheduler` with pipeline parallelism greater than one. PP1, synchronous scheduling, and MRV1 retain the existing effective limit of `max_num_seqs`.

This advances Workstream A of #50853.

### Why this is not a duplicate

#50410 is the only overlapping open PR. It caps the total number of scheduled requests, including prefill. On a matched Kimi-K3 + DSpark Mooncake replay, that global cap reduced output throughput by 8.21% versus natural scheduling. The decode-only policy here improved output throughput by 22.95% versus natural scheduling and by 33.95% versus #50410.

The distinction is implemented and tested explicitly: all 32 prompt-completing requests are scheduled together before decode is divided into two disjoint Q16 cohorts under PP2.

## Test Plan

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/v1/core/test_async_scheduler.py

pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py \
  vllm/v1/core/sched/async_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_async_scheduler.py
```

## Test Result

- Async scheduler tests: `20 passed`
- File-scoped pre-commit suite: passed, including Ruff, formatting, and mypy

Matched Kimi-K3 + DSpark serving results on B200:

| Workload | Topology | Natural cohorts | Balanced cohorts | Output tok/s change |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Fixed 64k/400, C64 | TP8/PP2 | Q19/Q13 | Q16/Q16 | +4.74% |
| Fixed 64k/400, C64 | TP8/PP4 | Q7/Q13/Q2/Q10 | Q8/Q8/Q8/Q8 | +12.62% |
| Mooncake trace, C64 | TP8/PP4 | natural | decode cap 8 | +22.95% |

The submitting human reviewed every changed line and the test results. AI assistance (OpenAI Codex) was used to implement the reviewed change, run validation, and prepare this PR description.

hits.title: [Feature]: Process-level PD Disaggregation within Single Instance
hits.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Description of the Feature Proposal
This proposal outlines a new scheduling and execution mechanism called "Process-level PD Disaggregation". The core idea is to spatially partition a single GPU's resources to run compute-bound prefill operations and memory-bound decode operations concurrently.

This is achieved by launching separate processes for prefill and decode on the same GPU, managed by NVIDIA MPS  and multiple stream. This approach enables resource sharing between the two distinct workloads, improving overall GPU utilization and allowing the system to meet strict SLOs for both TTFT and ITL.

### Motivation for the Proposal
LLM serving in production environments faces a critical challenge: simultaneously optimizing for TTFT and ITL. During traffic surges, single-instance deployments struggle to balance these two metrics, making it difficult to meet strict SLOs, such as TTFT < 1.3s and avg. ITL < 30ms. 

The prefill stage is typically compute-bound, while the decode stage is memory-bound, leading to inefficient use of GPU resources when these operations are scheduled sequentially. A promising approach is to overlap these two phases to maximize resource utilization. This feature aims to implement such an overlapping mechanism to solve the trade-off between TTFT and ITL.

### Specific Problem
I'm working on serving a Qwen2-32B model under high, concurrent traffic and need to maintain a high-quality user experience defined by strict SLOs.

Current strategies, such as chunked prefill, are insufficient. Chunked prefill breaks a large prefill request into smaller chunks and batches them with decode requests. While this method effectively reduces ITL and improves GPU utilization compared to a prefill-priority policy, it introduces a severe regression in TTFT.

To validate this in our production environment (average output length of 4K, average input length of 12K), we tested the impact of different chunk sizes. Our findings show a direct and problematic trade-off: smaller chunk sizes lower ITL but dramatically increase TTFT. This is because each subsequent chunk must re-access the KV cache generated by previous chunks, introducing significant memory access and scheduling overhead.

The data below illustrates this problem. As we decrease the chunk size , P99+ ITL improves, but average TTFT increases beyond our SLO of 1.3s.

| Chunk Size |  3K | 4K | 5K | No-Chunk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Average TTFT (ms) | 1445 | 1394 | 1299 | 1108.32 |
| Average ITL (ms) | 21 | 20 | 19 | 20.43 |
| P99 ITL (ms) | 227 | 274 | 297 | 400.31 |
| P99.2 ITL (ms) | 235 | 288 | 309 | 515.07 |
| P99.4 ITL (ms) | 242 | 302 | 329 | 675.18 |
| P99.6 ITL (ms) | 249 | 319 | 351 | 882.51 |
| P99.8 ITL (ms) | 262 | 336 | 374 | 1179.15 |
| Max ITL (ms) | 883 | 1036 | 1051 | 3950 |
| Requests with ITL > 400ms (%) | 4% | 39.40% | 72% | 82% |
| Stutters per Request | 1 | 1.29 | 2.22 | 3.85 |
| Stutter Rate (%) | 3.760% | 5.700% | 23.000% | 81.000% |
| Position of First Stutter | 204 | 269 | 228 | 92 |


### Resource Utilization in LLM
To understand the root cause, we profiled the SM utilization of different operations during the prefill stage on a vLLM 0.9.1 deployment (Qwen2-32B, 8 x H20). The results confirm that prefill is a compute-bound phase, with many kernels achieving high SM utilization. In contrast, the decode phase is memory-bound and exhibits consistently low SM utilization.

Prefill Stage SM Utilization (%) for Various Operations:
Operations | Kernel | 1k | 2k | 4k | 8k | 16k | 32k
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
Input RMS | fused_add_rms | 33.0 | 67.0 | 84.5 | 80.3 | 95.4 | 95.4
QKV | nvje | 88.3 | 89.2 | 97.1 | 93.8 | 99.3 | 95.8
Rotation Embedding | rotation_embeding | 92.0 | 73.0 | 90.0 | 85.0 | 93.0 | 91.7
Attention | reshape_and_cache | 92.0 | 73.0 | 90.0 | 85.0 | 93.0 | 96.0
  | fa_fwd | 78.1 | 71.0 | 70.3 | 86.4 | 89.3 | 99.0
  | fa_fwd_combine | 70.0 | 66.0 | 76.0 | 57.0 | 40.0 | 100.0
Row Parallel Linear | nvjet | 70.0 | 66.3 | 82.2 | 88.5 | 71.5 | 93.2
  | nccl | 35.5 | 33.3 | 30.7 | 28.1 | 23.2 | 21.9
Output RMS | fused_add_rms | 55.3 | 35.4 | 71.3 | 80.5 | 88.0 | 96.5
MLP | nvje | 91.5 | 94.7 | 98.0 | 98.9 | 98.8 | 99.6
  | silu | 92.4 | 82.0 | 87.6 | 87.3 | 97.2 | 99.2
  | nvtj | 92.8 | 94.8 | 96.4 | 98.2 | 96.9 | 95.8
  | nccl | 34.3 | 44.9 | 26.2 | 24.9 | 22.2 | 46.8

The low utilization during communication  and the memory-bound nature of decode create a significant opportunity for optimization. By allowing prefill and decode to share GPU resources spatially, we can service high-priority decode requests while backfilling the GPU with compute-intensive prefill work.

### Proposed Solution
Inspired by concepts from works like Semi-PD, we propose implementing intra-instance prefill/decode disaggregation. This involves the following core features:

1. Multi-Process Architecture: For each GPU, we will launch two independent processes: one for Prefill and one for Decode. NVIDIA MPS will be used to enable spatial sharing of the GPU hardware, allowing kernels from both processes to execute concurrently.
2. Multi-Stream Execution: The Prefill and Decode processes will be mapped to separate CUDA streams. This allows the hardware to overlap operations.
3. Unified Cross-Process Memory Management: A unified memory manager will be created to handle the KV cache. This manager will use CUDA IPC to share GPU memory handles between the Prefill and Decode processes, ensuring the Decode process can seamlessly read the KV cache generated by the Prefill process.
4. SM Controller: It will dynamically modify the SM mask in the Thread Management Descriptor to control which kernels execute on which TPCs.
5. SLO-Aware Scheduler: The central scheduler will be enhanced to: 1) Route incoming requests to the Prefill and Decode processes. 2)Use an integrated simulator to predict the execution time of prefill and decode tasks. 3) Dynamically adjust the SM resource allocation based on current load and SLO targets.
6. Layer-wise Chunked Prefill: To avoid the high overhead of token-level chunking, prefill computation will be chunked at the layer level. This allows a long prefill to be paused and resumed between layers, creating opportunities for the scheduler to execute high-priority decode batches. A brief sleep or yield mechanism will be added to the prefill loop to ensure the Decode process can preemptively seize resources during contention.


Our proposed approach has been preliminarily implemented and validated on the sglang, where it has already demonstrated promising performance gains in balancing TTFT and ITL under our workload. This work is further detailed in our paper, "Boosting LLM Serving through Spatial-Temporal GPU Resource Sharing" and the proof-of-concept implementation is available at: https://github.com/zejia-lin/BulletServe.

We are currently in the process of refactoring and hardening the system for production use. We believe this “Process-level Prefill/Decode Disaggregation within a Single Instance” feature would be a valuable addition to vLLM. We are keen to collaborate with the community to integrate this functionality, enhancing vLLM's capabilities for serving mission-critical, low-latency LLM applications.

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

hits.title: [RFC]: Complete Model Runner V2 pipeline parallelism: scheduling, speculative decoding, and PP-first DP/EP topology
hits.body:
### Motivation.

> [!NOTE]
> This RFC expands the original request-admission proposal into an end-to-end plan for Model Runner V2 (MRV2) pipeline-parallel feature composition. The original proposal remains Workstream A below, with its prototype in #50410.

MRV2 pipeline parallelism (PP) already overlaps multiple batches to reduce pipeline bubbles (#42187). With asynchronous scheduling, it keeps `pp_size + 1` batch slots in flight, while a decode request becomes eligible again after a `pp_size`-step cadence.

That foundation works for basic generation, but the surrounding features do not yet compose cleanly with PP:

| Area | Current state | Gap addressed by this RFC |
|---|---|---|
| Request scheduling | Basic MRV2 PP works | A burst can fill the global request slots in one batch and leave later PP batches empty |
| MTP speculative decoding | Work is in progress | Drafts produced and applied locally on the last rank must be published to non-last ranks and restored for the still-live rows of the stored step-`T` feedback slot |
| EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark | Explicitly rejected with PP in MRV2 today | Auxiliary hidden states may be produced on earlier ranks but are consumed by the proposer on the last rank |
| Index-sharing models | Rank-local buffers work when producer and consumer are colocated | A PP cut may fall between an index producer and a layer that reuses its top-k indices |
| PP + DP/EP topology | Current deployments commonly place complete DP replicas contiguously | On multiple nodes this tends to keep PP local while DP/EP groups cross nodes; a PP-first placement should keep EP/TP inside a node and move PP traffic across nodes |

The common theme is that PP is not only a partition of model layers. It also creates two state-transfer paths with different direction and lifetime:

1. **forward state**, sent from one PP rank to the next for the current microbatch; and
2. **deferred result state**, applied locally on the last rank and published to non-last ranks, which consume the stored `PPHandler` FIFO slot `pp_size` local feedback-ring steps later.

Adding each new tensor with one-off communication code would make ordering, CUDA-graph capture, request-slot reuse, and multi-node topology assumptions increasingly fragile. This RFC therefore proposes both the missing feature support and a small declarative PP transport abstraction that can carry future optional state without redesigning the execution loop each time.

#### Goals

- Balance request admission across concurrent MRV2 PP batches.
- Define correct MRV2 PP composition with MTP, EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark speculative decoding.
- Carry auxiliary hidden states and cross-partition index-sharing state when a model partition requires them.
- Define a PP-first multi-node placement in which each node hosts one complete PP stage's DP/EP domain, keeping EP/TP communication intra-node and PP communication inter-node.
- Keep optional communication absent when a model or configuration does not need it.
- Preserve static, graph-friendly buffer schemas and minimize extra collectives.

#### Non-goals

- Changing Model Runner V1.
- Introducing a new speculative decoding algorithm.
- Redesigning DP request routing, real/dummy execution cadence, or wave draining, or migrating live request/KV state between DP lanes.
- Introducing a new pipeline schedule such as interleaved 1F1B.
- Requiring every model to emit auxiliary hidden states or index buffers.
- Enabling adaptive verification with PP in the first rollout; it needs a separate protocol for trimmed shapes, confidence/cost state, and rank agreement.
- Supporting a PP-stage DP/EP footprint that cannot fit in a node-local topology domain in the first rollout.

### Proposed Change.

Implement the RFC as four independently reviewable workstreams over one set of communication and correctness invariants.

```text
                    current-microbatch forward plane
  scheduler  ->  PP rank 0  ->  ...  ->  PP rank N (sample + propose)
                    | IntermediateTensors | aux hidden states | shared indices |
                    |
                    +<---------- deferred result plane ----------+
                       sampled/count metadata and optional drafts
                       (queued in the worker-side PPHandler feedback FIFO)

  PP-first multi-node placement:

  node 0 / PP stage 0: [DP0 ... DPN]  <- EP/TP stays node-local
                              |  PP lanes  |
  node 1 / PP stage 1: [DP0 ... DPN]  <- EP/TP stays node-local
```

#### Workstream A: balance request admission across PP batches

Within each scheduler/DP replica, the scheduler currently applies `max_num_seqs` as one global running-request limit and greedily fills a batch until an existing token, sequence, KV-cache, or model-specific constraint is reached. A burst of short, uniform requests can therefore consume all local request slots before the pipeline has formed multiple useful batches.

For example:

```text
pipeline_parallel_size = 2
max_num_seqs = 25
50 short requests arrive together
```

The current scheduler can produce `25, 0, 25, 0` scheduled requests over four steps. The prototype in #50410 instead caps the next batch at:

```python
num_requests = min(
    max_num_running_reqs,
    get_num_unfinished_requests(),
)
max_num_scheduled_reqs = ceil(num_requests / pp_size)
```

The prototype applies the cap to both requests already in `RUNNING` and admissions from `WAITING`, while all existing token, KV-cache, priority, preemption, structured-output, and model-specific constraints remain authoritative. In the example, the first two useful batches become approximately `13, 12` instead of `25, 0`.

The divisor is `pp_size`, not `pp_size + 1`: the additional asynchronous queue entry covers result propagation and scheduler/worker overlap rather than an additional compute stage. Non-final chunked-prefill chunks remain eligible in adjacent steps because they do not depend on sampled-token feedback.

This is intentionally a PP batch target, not a claim that request count always equals compute. Request count is a useful decode proxy; scheduled tokens are a better prefill proxy.

The proposed MVP differs from the current prototype in one important respect: already-eligible `RUNNING` decode keeps its existing scheduling behavior, while the balance target is a soft cap on **new/resumed admission from `WAITING`**. The target may be exceeded when later phases have no runnable work, at low concurrency, at a KV/capacity boundary, or to prevent priority starvation. This preserves work conservation and avoids delaying active decode solely to make phase widths look uniform.

Every DP replica computes this target locally. Evaluation should decide whether the final policy is request-count based, token based, or hybrid, and whether a persistent phase assignment is worth its complexity around completion, abort, preemption, resume, and priority changes.

#### Workstream B: make PP state transport extensible

Refactor PP state ownership into a small declarative module. `PPTransport`, `ForwardPayload`, and `DeferredResultPayload` below are conceptual names, not a required public API.

One ownership module describes two independent schemas and communicators:

**1. Forward payload: adjacent rank -> adjacent rank, current microbatch**

- opaque model `IntermediateTensors` such as `hidden_states` and `residual`;
- namespaced sidecars for auxiliary hidden states keyed by a global activation-boundary ID and configured slot;
- a namespaced active top-k/index sidecar when the partition boundary crosses an index-reuse dependency.

**2. Deferred result payload: last PP rank -> every non-last PP rank, delayed receiver slot**

- sampled tokens;
- sampled/rejected-token counts;
- optional next-step draft tokens;
- local queued request mappings and generation metadata that associate the received rows with still-live request slots (these do not need to be network fields).

Each adjacent forward edge has its own field/liveness plan; the existing `PPHandler` sibling broadcast has one group-consistent feedback plan. They share descriptor and lifecycle machinery but not communicator, stream, cadence, or participant set. A conceptual field descriptor is:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PPTensorSpec:
    name: str
    plane: Literal["forward", "deferred_result"]
    boundary_id: int | None
    slot: int | None
    dtype: torch.dtype
    trailing_shape: tuple[int, ...]
    tp_policy: Literal["replicated", "sharded", "direct"]
    carry: Literal[
        "one_edge", "until_last", "until_consumed", "feedback_group"
    ]
    lifetime: Literal["forward_execution", "delayed_request_state"]
```

The exact fields can differ. The correctness MVP should run the declared plan over the existing tensor-dict path:

- namespace and split opaque model tensors from optional sidecars;
- keep each edge's field presence, key, dtype, slot ordering, carry policy, and TP policy deterministic after initialization;
- export/import sidecars through model-specific adapters;
- retain current tensor-dict metadata and allocation behavior where required for backend compatibility;
- stream/event ownership and buffer reuse centralized in the transport module;
- request generation/slot checks retained for delayed feedback, so an aborted or replaced request cannot consume stale state;
- group-identical feedback row order, row count, dtype/shape, collective order, and whole-collective skip decisions; no branch on rank-local optional-field presence;
- optional fields disabled add no bytes or collectives beyond the existing forward and sampled/count feedback paths.

For forward sidecars, `N` means the execution row count after padding (`num_tokens_after_padding` / the batch execution descriptor), not only logical scheduled tokens. Buffers and wire shapes use `N`; adapters separately track which rows contain real tokens.

For the initial models in this RFC, auxiliary hidden states are TP-replicated, and shared top-k is TP-replicated `[N, index_topk]` `torch.int32`. Existing model tensors such as sequence-parallel residual state retain their direct/sharded policy. Because the current tensor-dict path may automatically slice/all-gather based on tensor size, sidecar policy must be explicit rather than inferred from divisibility.

Model-specific adapters should declare which sidecars a partition boundary needs, export locally produced fields, and import received fields into the correct persistent model buffer. The communication layer should not interpret EAGLE, DSpark, or model-specific index semantics. Namespaced wire keys such as `model/*`, `spec/aux_hidden_states`, and `model/shared_index_topk` can avoid collisions while keeping ordinary model tensors opaque.

A later performance phase may compile a static wire schema, use persistent graph-address-stable receive buffers, and remove per-step CPU metadata. That requires explicit lower-level `GroupCoordinator`/backend protocol work and is not implied by adding the correctness wrapper.

Compatible small fields should be packed when doing so removes latency-sensitive collectives, following the direction explored in draft #47686. Large auxiliary tensors should not be blindly packed with token metadata: grouping must respect direction, dtype, destination, lifetime, TP layout, and performance. The abstraction is unified at the ownership/schema layer, while the two data planes remain separate internally.

#### Workstream C: compose PP with speculative decoding

##### C1. Base MTP draft-feedback synchronization

Under MRV2 asynchronous scheduling, scheduler-side speculative token IDs are shape placeholders: their authoritative values remain in per-worker GPU request state. The speculative proposer runs on the last PP rank. Every stage's sampled/draft/sequence bookkeeping must nevertheless describe the same logical token sequence: the first stage materializes the correct sampled-plus-draft token IDs, while later stages consume the corresponding forward activations and attention metadata.

Here `pp_feedback_step` means a local worker execute/control step that advances the `PPHandler` FIFO. It is not an EngineCore asynchronous batch-queue slot and is not advanced by a MoE DP dummy forward.

#52295 implements the narrow synchronization piece. The last rank applies sampled state locally in feedback step `T`, runs proposal, retains its new draft state, and then publishes one feedback record to non-last ranks. The token wire payload is fixed at `[B, (K + 1) + K] = [B, 2K + 1]` (`int64` sampled plus draft columns), while the existing `[2, B]` (`int32`) sampled/rejected count collective remains. Draft synchronization therefore adds `K` token-ID columns per request but no new collective.

Each non-last rank posts the matching receive in feedback step `T`, queues it with the saved row mapping, need mask, and slot-generation snapshot, and applies the surviving rows at feedback step `T + pp_size`. Sampled and draft rows use the same liveness/generation decision; invalid draft rows are compacted before index-copy because a `-1` destination is not valid for that operation. The association comes from FIFO feedback-step order and the saved step-`T` metadata, not from the composition of the current batch at `T + pp_size`.

The required invariant is:

> The last stage applies its sampling outcome and derived next-step drafts locally in feedback step `T` and publishes them as one causally consistent record. Every non-last stage posts the matching receive in step `T` and applies the stored live rows at feedback step `T + pp_size`, before that request's next verification input is prepared.

#52295 should be treated as the base transport/state-synchronization change, not as the complete enablement of every MTP model. Its transport gate is PP plus any speculative configuration that has already passed validation, so this feedback mechanism should not be duplicated per speculative method. Broader model-specific work in #46994 includes PP capability declarations, model-specific projection paths, weight/embedding ownership, and a same-rank stale sparse-MLA buffer-reference fix. Those requirements should either land with the affected model or be guarded by an explicit support check; the same-rank buffer fix is distinct from the cross-rank dependency in C3.

Fixed wire width also needs an explicit validity/padding protocol for a normal `[B, 1]` no-draft or prefill sampler source; `num_sampled` determines which sampled columns are valid. Existing #52295 coverage consists of two CPU/mock tests for payload splitting/event waiting and draft slot writeback. Real multi-rank communication, fixed-width send/receive, `T -> T + pp_size`, partial abort/reuse, and mixed prefill/decode are merge/enablement criteria, not established behavior. Delaying broadcast until after proposal may also change overlap, so validation must include TPOT and proposer latency.

##### C2. EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark auxiliary hidden states

These methods require auxiliary target-model hidden states during proposal. MRV2 currently rejects EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark with PP before execution. If those guards were simply removed, each rank would capture only its local auxiliary outputs and a non-last rank would return ordinary `IntermediateTensors` without carrying those outputs, so the proposer on the last rank would still see incomplete state.

For a configured set of auxiliary layers:

1. normalize each capture point to a global **activation-boundary ID** (`0` for the state before the first layer and `layer_idx + 1` for the state after that layer), including method-specific `+1` conversions;
2. map boundary IDs to the draft configuration's fixed slot order rather than numerically sorting IDs;
3. when an auxiliary state is produced, add it to the forward payload;
4. carry it through subsequent PP boundaries with `until_last` liveness;
5. combine upstream and last-rank-local states in configured slot order;
6. pass the ordered states to the proposer on the last PP rank.

Auxiliary states are forward dependencies of the current microbatch, not delayed sampled-token feedback. They should therefore use the adjacent-rank forward plane and must not be added to the last-rank-to-non-last-ranks feedback broadcast.

The schema must support zero, one, or multiple auxiliary tensors, and partition tests must cover auxiliary boundaries on the first, middle, and last PP ranks. Implementations that pack compatible states may use a stable `[N, slots, hidden]` layout where `N` is the padded execution row count, but correctness must not depend on all states having identical shapes. Persistent receive/pack buffers are a performance-phase optimization for avoiding per-step allocation and address changes under CUDA graphs.

Transport is necessary but not sufficient to remove the current PP guards. Model-specific enablement must also normalize activation-boundary IDs and target layer counts to global (not stage-local) coordinates, validate draft embedding/head ownership on the last rank, and remove loader-level PP rejections only after the corresponding model path is tested.

##### C3. Index-sharing state across a PP cut

Some models compute top-k routing/index information in one layer and reuse it in later layers. For example, an index-sharing pattern may contain one producing layer followed by layers that skip top-k computation and read a persistent buffer.

If PP cuts between that producer and a consumer in the same reuse interval, a rank-local buffer on the downstream rank has not been populated for the current microbatch. The forward schema must then carry the active top-k buffer across one or more reuse-only stages until it is consumed or overwritten.

At model/partition initialization, dependency analysis should determine whether a boundary crosses an index-reuse interval:

- if it does not, no extra tensor is registered;
- if it does, register the current contract—TP-replicated `[N, index_topk]` `torch.int32`, where `N` is the padded execution row count—and copy it into the downstream persistent shared buffer before model/graph execution;
- tie buffer validity and lifetime to the forward microbatch/transport handle so data cannot leak between in-flight batches;
- allow future model adapters to declare other trailing dimensions or dtypes without weakening this RFC's concrete acceptance contract.

This cross-rank dependency is distinct from the stale-buffer-reference issue addressed by parts of #46994 when draft and target models share an indexer on the same rank. Both must be correct, but only the former requires PP-boundary transport.

As an initial safety fallback, unsupported partitions may fail early with a precise error. The intended final behavior is to transport the dependency rather than permanently constraining PP cuts to index-reuse boundaries.

#### Workstream D: PP-first DP/EP topology for multi-node serving

This workstream is about **physical partition and placement order**, not a new DP load-balancing, dummy-forward, or drain protocol. Each request remains sticky to one logical DP lane, and that lane still traverses one complete PP pipeline. The proposal first assigns nodes to PP stages, then places the stage's DP/EP (and TP, when used) ranks inside that node.

##### D1. Background: why DP-first placement is suboptimal for multi-node MoE

With a conventional DP-first placement, complete DP replicas are packed before moving to the next node. Consider two 8-GPU nodes with `PP=2`, `DP=8`, and `TP=1`:

```text
default physical placement

node 0: DP0{PP0,PP1} DP1{PP0,PP1} DP2{PP0,PP1} DP3{PP0,PP1}
node 1: DP4{PP0,PP1} DP5{PP0,PP1} DP6{PP0,PP1} DP7{PP0,PP1}
```

This keeps several PP pipelines entirely inside a node, but the fixed-PP DP/EP domain spans both nodes. For MoE models, expert dispatch/combine is an all-to-all or all-gather/reduce-scatter style hot path repeated throughout the model. Sending that traffic across the inter-node fabric is substantially more topology-sensitive than keeping it on NVLink/NVSwitch.

PP communication has a different shape: each logical DP lane sends activations across an ordered stage boundary, with small sampled/draft feedback in the reverse PP direction. This traffic is point-to-point or PP-scoped, regular, and can be overlapped with pipeline execution. It is therefore the preferable communication dimension to place across nodes.

##### D2. Proposed PP-first placement

Place one complete PP stage's `DP x PCP x TP` footprint in a node-local topology domain before allocating the next PP stage:

```text
PP-first physical placement

node 0 / PP0: DP0 DP1 DP2 DP3 DP4 DP5 DP6 DP7
                    |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
                    +--- matching cross-node PP lanes ---+
node 1 / PP1: DP0 DP1 DP2 DP3 DP4 DP5 DP6 DP7
```

The resulting communication placement is:

- `EP(pp)` stays inside the node containing that PP stage;
- `TP(pp, dp, pcp)` also stays inside that stage's node-local domain;
- `PP(dp, pcp, tp)` connects matching coordinates across nodes in stage order;
- PP forward activations, optional sidecars from Workstream B, and small sampled/draft feedback are the steady-state model data that crosses nodes;
- control-plane coordination may still cross nodes and is not the optimization target of this workstream.

The physical placement can be PP-first without changing the logical identity of a DP lane. Scheduler, request, KV-cache, sampling, and speculative state remain owned by that lane; no request or KV state is migrated between DP lanes.

##### D3. Topology contract and scope

The first rollout should target a uniform topology with one complete PP stage per node. Its contract is:

- the stage footprint `DP x PCP x TP` fits completely in one node-local communication domain;
- every EP and TP group is node-local;
- each PP group contains matching `(dp, pcp, tp)` coordinates in increasing stage order;
- every logical worker is placed exactly once, with no duplicated or missing device;
- a requested placement that would spill an EP group across nodes fails before model execution;
- disabling PP-first placement preserves the existing topology.

Multiple complete stage blocks may share a node in a future extension, provided no EP/TP group is split across nodes. A stage footprint larger than one node, heterogeneous partial-stage placement, PCP+DP combinations that are otherwise unsupported, and elastic-EP composition are outside the initial scope.

The existing DP/EP execution-order rules remain unchanged: ranks in a coupled EP domain must still enter model collectives consistently, and an idle logical DP lane still follows the existing dummy-execution behavior. These are compatibility requirements, not the feature proposed here.

#### Cross-cutting correctness invariants

1. **Verification-state agreement:** every PP stage agrees on ordered request rows and logical token/position/spec-verification metadata; the first stage materializes the correct token IDs and downstream stages consume the corresponding stage-local forward state.
2. **Forward-dependency completeness:** the consumer of an auxiliary state or shared index sees the value produced for the same microbatch.
3. **Slot safety:** aborted, preempted, or replaced requests cannot consume delayed state from an earlier slot generation.
4. **Placement completeness:** every logical `(pp, dp, pcp, tp)` worker maps to exactly one physical device, and every selected device has exactly one owner.
5. **Topology locality:** in PP-first mode every EP/TP group is contained in one node-local communication domain, while PP groups connect matching coordinates in stage order.
6. **PP-lane isolation:** PP P2P and optional sidecars stay inside one logical DP lane and follow the per-edge transport plan.
7. **Feedback collective agreement:** every feedback participant uses group-identical row ordering, row count, dtype/shape, collective order, and whole-collective skip decisions for a feedback step.
8. **DP/EP execution compatibility:** changing physical placement does not change existing collective-order, dummy-execution, or execution-shape rules for a coupled EP domain.
9. **State isolation:** request, KV, sampling, and speculative state remain inside one sticky DP lane; PP transfer is not DP migration.
10. **Work conservation:** a soft balance target cannot indefinitely create empty PP phases while runnable work exists, and scheduler safety/fairness constraints take precedence.
11. **Feature transparency:** optional fields disabled add no bytes or collectives beyond the existing PP forward and sampled/count feedback paths; disabling PP-first placement preserves current topology.
12. **MRV1/non-PP compatibility:** this RFC does not change their scheduling or communication semantics.

#### Rollout plan

1. Adapt the request-balancing prototype and scheduler tests from #50410 to the soft, work-conserving `WAITING`-admission MVP, then validate its policy/performance.
2. Introduce the ownership/adapter layer over the existing tensor-dict forward path and `PPHandler` feedback path without changing basic-generation behavior.
3. Land the base MTP draft-state synchronization from #52295, plus model-specific enablement or guards identified by #46994.
4. Add auxiliary-hidden-state descriptors and enable EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark model by model.
5. Add partition dependency analysis and cross-rank top-k/index transfer for index-sharing models.
6. Validate the PP-first multi-node topology contract, including node-local EP/TP groups and cross-node PP lanes.
7. Independently evaluate the static-wire/persistent-buffer transport performance phase.

Steps that are independent may proceed in parallel, but every step should preserve the invariants above and keep unsupported combinations behind an early, actionable validation error.

#### Compatibility and initial support limits

- Target and draft model paths must explicitly satisfy PP capability, loader, projection, embedding/head ownership, and partition checks before their guard is removed.
- Adaptive verification plus PP remains unsupported in the initial rollout.
- Existing restrictions such as MRV2 PP with an external launcher, elastic EP with PP, and `PCP > 1` with `DP > 1` remain unchanged unless a separate RFC/PR addresses them.
- `max_num_seqs` remains a per-EngineCore/per-DP-replica limit.
- A draft model without its own embedding/head must either have a validated last-rank loading/aliasing path or fail early when the corresponding target component is a `PPMissingLayer`.
- Initial PP-first support requires a uniform topology in which one complete `DP x PCP x TP` stage footprint fits inside one node-local communication domain.

#### Alternatives considered

1. **Add model-specific tensors directly to each send/receive call.** This is smaller initially but duplicates buffer, ordering, and lifecycle logic and does not scale to the next optional state.
2. **Put every optional tensor in one always-present payload.** This simplifies branching but wastes memory/bandwidth and makes high-volume forward state share an unsuitable lifetime with small delayed token metadata.
3. **Use a separate collective for every field.** Simple semantically, but latency grows with features; #47686 shows why packing small PP feedback fields can matter.
4. **Force PP cuts to dependency boundaries.** Useful as a temporary guard, but reduces partition flexibility and can produce poor memory/compute balance.
5. **Send auxiliary hidden states directly from their producer to the last rank.** This creates a variable communication graph; forwarding through adjacent boundaries keeps ownership and ordering aligned with the existing pipeline.
6. **Keep DP-first physical placement.** This preserves current deployment behavior but can force EP traffic across nodes while underusing PP as the inter-node communication dimension.
7. **Use hierarchical cross-node EP collectives.** This may reduce the penalty but does not provide the same hard node-local EP/TP boundary and remains backend/topology dependent.
8. **Allow arbitrary heterogeneous stage placement immediately.** More flexible, but substantially harder to validate and reason about than a uniform one-stage-per-node first rollout.

#### Evaluation plan

**Correctness matrix**

- PP sizes 2 and 4; DP sizes 1, 2, 4, and 8; TP 1/2 and representative EP configurations;
- synchronous and asynchronous scheduling; eager and compiled/full-CUDA-graph execution;
- no speculation, MTP, EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark;
- speculative widths 1, 2, and 3, including no-draft/prefill feedback rows;
- auxiliary layers before, on, and after PP boundaries;
- PP cuts outside and inside an index-reuse interval;
- burst admission, mixed prefill/decode, chunked prefill, preemption, abort storms, pause/resume, and request-slot reuse;
- two 8-GPU nodes with `PP=2, DP=8, TP=1`;
- two 8-GPU nodes with `PP=2, DP=4, TP=2`;
- a representative `PP=4` topology;
- both default DP-first and proposed PP-first physical placements.

The model-level acceptance set should include:

- Llama/Qwen EAGLE3 for global activation-boundary ID and configured-slot ordering;
- DeepSeek V3.2 with a forced PP cut inside a producer-to-reuse interval;
- DeepSeek V4 DSpark for post-mHC-mean auxiliary state;
- Kimi K3 DSpark/EAGLE3 for model-specific attention-residual auxiliary state;
- a draft model without its own embedding/head, covering either the validated last-rank loading path or the expected fail-fast error.

Use synthetic/unit tests for exact transport contents, schema validation, boundary liveness, activation-boundary slot ordering, request generations, and topology membership. Add real multi-rank tests for `T -> T + pp_size` feedback cadence, abort/reuse filtering, fixed-width payloads, forward sidecars, and collective traces. Multi-node tests must collect actual node identities for every PP/DP/EP/TP group and prove that PP-first mode keeps EP/TP node-local. Representative end-to-end models should cover output parity and speculative acceptance; supported configurations should be compared with PP=1 using deterministic inputs where possible. Require no deadlock or collective-order mismatch under timeout/failure-injection tests.

**Performance metrics**

- requests and scheduled tokens per PP batch;
- per-stage idle time and pipeline bubbles;
- throughput, TTFT, and TPOT;
- speculative acceptance rate and proposer latency;
- PP bytes, collective/P2P count, and communication overlap;
- CUDA-graph memory and capture/replay stability;
- inter-node bytes attributed to PP forward/feedback versus EP/TP collectives;
- EP all-to-all latency, PP overlap, node-local GPU utilization, and topology-induced idle time;
- preemption count and KV-cache utilization.

Optional transport disabled should have no material regression against current basic PP. Enabled configurations should be compared both before/after packing so communication optimizations remain evidence-driven.

#### Related work

- MRV2 pipeline bubble reduction and current PP/DP foundation: #42187
- Request-admission balancing prototype: #50410
- Isolated MTP draft-token synchronization: #52295
- Broader MTP-over-PP enablement and model-specific fixes: #46994
- Packed PP sampled/count/draft feedback draft experiment: #47686
- Async scheduling plan: #27679
- Persistent batch redesign: #23446
- Long-context optimized PP RFC: #41685
- Chunked pipeline parallel RFC: #33914

The long-context and chunked-PP RFCs focus on splitting long-context work, asynchronous P2P, and dynamic chunking. This RFC focuses on composing the existing MRV2 PP execution model with scheduler admission, speculative state, index-sharing dependencies, and a PP-first multi-node DP/EP topology.

#### Open questions

1. Should the transport API extend `PPHandler` and `IntermediateTensors`, or should both become clients of a new internal `PPTransport` owner?
2. Which small fields should be packed, and what static layout/versioning is needed for full CUDA graphs?
3. Should auxiliary hidden states remain individually keyed by activation-boundary/slot or use one packed tensor plus offsets?
4. Should cross-boundary index state be transported for all supported models, or should the first rollout reject unsafe partition cuts?
5. Should PP admission balance requests, tokens, estimated compute, or a hybrid, and should it be opt-in initially?
6. Should PP-first placement be explicit-only at first, or selected automatically when the stage footprint matches node capacity?
7. Must the initial topology require exactly one PP stage per node, or may a node host multiple complete stage blocks?
8. If an EP domain cannot fit in one node, should configuration fail, fall back to DP-first placement, or require an explicitly selected hierarchical EP mode?
9. Which feature combinations are required before removing the current PP validation guards for EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark?

### Feedback Period.

2026-08-18 through 2026-09-01.

### CC List.

@njhill @WoosukKwon @robertgshaw2-redhat @heheda12345 @youkaichao @eastwood-c @ChihayaK @yewentao256

### Any Other Things.

The author can provide scheduler traces, device profiles, representative PP partition layouts, and acceptance-rate results for the proposed combinations. Feedback is especially welcome on the transport ownership boundary, the minimum support matrix for the first rollout, and whether index-sharing dependencies should initially be transported or guarded by partition validation.

hits.title: [Performance]: [MRV2][PP]: Post sampled-result receives closer to T+PP consumption
hits.body: ## Proposal to improve performance ### TL;DR - In MRV2 pipeline parallelism, non-last ranks can post sampled-result receives several local feedback steps before consumption. A receiver-side NCCL kernel can remain active while independent model work runs. - Deferring PP4 receivers by three feedback steps improved output throughput by approximately 18% on a short-generation, prefill-heavy workload and by 4--6% on two decode-heavy workload classes, with all requests completing. - Moving a due delayed receive from before to after the current model execution produced another 4.8% gain on the prefill-heavy workload in a same-configuration comparison and nearly eliminated sampled-result receive/model overlap in the captured PP0 window. - The current best jointly tuned configuration combines delay 3, post-model launch, and a retuned PP partition. Relative to the earlier delay-3 configurations, it improves output throughput by approximately 5--11% across the three workload classes. Those numbers are combined tuning results, not isolated post-model effects. - Draft PR [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948) currently contains the deferred-receive prototype only. The post-model ordering experiment is a separate follow-up prototype and is not yet in that PR. ### Summary Model Runner V2 pipeline parallelism returns sampled results from the last PP rank to every non-last rank. The CUDA implementation uses a sibling process group and side stream, as introduced by [#42187](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42187). However, a non-last rank posts its receive in local feedback step `T`, while the result is not consumed until `T + pp_size`. If the last rank has not produced the result yet, the receiver-side NCCL broadcast kernel can remain active across several intervening model executions. A side stream removes default-stream ordering, but does not isolate GPU execution and communication resources. The pending receive can therefore slow otherwise independent model work. If its CUDA event is still incomplete at `T + pp_size`, the main stream must also wait before applying the sampled result. This issue proposes an opt-in just-in-time receiver policy: - keep the last rank's source broadcast at its current point; - save receive metadata at feedback step `T`; - post non-last-rank receives closer to consumption; and - preserve the existing `T + pp_size` event wait as the correctness fallback. For `pp_size=4`, the first prototype uses delay 3: ```text Current: T post recv [possibly resident----------------------] consume at T+4 Deferred: T save receive metadata T+3 post recv [-------] consume at T+4 ``` A follow-up variant keeps delay 3 but posts the due receive *after* the current model execution instead of immediately before it: ```text T+3 before-model: post recv -> model work -> consume later T+3 post-model: model work -> post recv -> consume later ``` The follow-up does not add another scheduler-step delay. It changes only the ordering within the due local step, reducing the final interval in which the receiver kernel can overlap model work. Implementation status: - Draft PR [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948) contains the opt-in receiver-delay implementation. - The post-model ordering variant is currently a separate experimental patch. Its results should not be interpreted as validation of the current PR head. ### Trace-guided mechanism The following reconstruction shows the two distinct costs. The long receive lifetimes are not equivalent to wire-transfer time or to one continuous hard wait: several pending receives can overlap model work, and only an event that is still incomplete at consumption causes the correctness wait. An older causal reconstruction also shows why CPU `execute_model` annotations must not be read as GPU execution boundaries. GPU work can lag host enqueue, while a receiver-side broadcast remains active. The red spans below are receiver-kernel lifetimes, not approximately 900 ms of payload transfer. ### Three mechanisms that should not be conflated 1. **Pending-receive interference.** A receiver collective is active while independent model work runs. Deferred or post-model posting targets this cost. 2. **Correctness wait.** At `T + pp_size`, the main stream must wait if the sampled result is still unavailable. Receiver deferral must preserve this wait and must not hide an increase in it. 3. **EngineCore queue depth.** MRV2 normally queues `pp_size + 1` batches to overlap host scheduling and worker execution. This extra queue entry does not change the sampled-result consume cadence of `pp_size` steps or shorten an already-posted receive. ### What the traces establish In two immediate-receive PP4 profiles, roughly one third of eligible sampled results were still incomplete when observed at their `T+4` consume point. The resulting hard waits were large enough to be visible as pipeline holes. This does **not** prove that PP3 compute alone was late. An incomplete event means that the complete source/collective/receiver path had not finished. Source production, stream backlog, transport progress, or receiver progress can all contribute. Deferral also changes the meaning of this metric. With delay 3, the receiver joins near local step `T+3`, and receiver launch is ordered after already enqueued local main-stream work. An incomplete event at `T+4` can therefore also mean that the receiver was posted too late in physical time to finish. Immediate- and delay-3 unready rates must not be compared as if both measured only source lateness. Nsight Systems establishes overlap and receiver-stage slowdown, but it does not identify the exact contested GPU resource. SM residency, warp scheduling, cache or memory traffic, and NCCL progress remain hypotheses until supported by lower-level counters. ### Result provenance The headline historical delay-3 and post-model experiments used a derived artifact based on vLLM revision [`ac7509e2`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/ac7509e2b1db). They establish the performance mechanism on that source line, but they are not performance measurements of the current PR head on current `main`. PR #53948 was separately tested on an official nightly based on revision [`46638857`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/46638857fdbb30e0c232c9e8f9cb1ff6d6f545c3). For the same short-generation, prefill-heavy workload class, delay 3 produced a 16.1% relative gain over immediate receive. Absolute throughput was lower than on the older source line before and after enabling delay 3, so current-main performance remains a separate issue from the deferred-receive mechanism. ### Immediate receive versus delay 3 The primary experiment used the public Kimi-K3 model in a multi-node PP4 configuration with Model Runner V2, asynchronous scheduling, CUDA graphs, Marlin MoE, FlashInfer autotuning, no expert parallelism, and no prefix cache. Each row compares otherwise equivalent runs for that workload class; scheduling limits were tuned by class. | Generic workload class | Delay-3 output-throughput change | Completion | |---|---:|---:| | Short generation, prefill-heavy | **approximately +18%** | All requests | | Long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +4%** | All requests | | Very long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +5%** | All requests | For the prefill-heavy workload, a matched Nsight capture showed: | Metric | Observed change with delay 3 | |---|---:| | Interior PP0 gaps at least 500 ms | **Eliminated in the capture** | | Largest interior PP0 gap | **Reduced by approximately 76%** | | PP0 median model time | **Reduced by approximately 21%** | | PP1 median model time | **Reduced by approximately 30%** | | PP2 median model time | **Reduced by approximately 22%** | | PP3 median model time | Approximately unchanged | The unchanged PP3 time is consistent with the mechanism: PP3 is the source, whereas PP0--PP2 are early receivers. All three non-last ranks participate; PP0 tends to expose the pause most clearly because it reaches the feedback dependency first, while PP1 and PP2 can hide part of the wait behind upstream activation dependencies. ### Before-model versus post-model launch Delay 3 still leaves approximately one local scheduler step in which the receive can overlap model execution. A follow-up prefill-heavy experiment moved the due receive from before to after current model execution. The following full-window runs used the same short-generation, prefill-heavy workload, image, PP partition, scheduling limits, receive delay, and concurrency. Both runs completed all requests. | Due receive placement | Output throughput | Total throughput | p50 latency | p99 latency | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Before model execution | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | | **After model execution** | **+4.8%** | **+4.8%** | **-5.9%** | **-5.5%** | These are same-configuration runs, not a serialized same-allocation A/B, so the result should be reproduced before treating 4.8% as a general gain. A separate pair of Nsight captures provides stronger mechanism evidence but is not a throughput A/B: both used delay 3 and the same PP partition, while the sequence-admission limit differed. | Receive placement | PP0 model time | PP1 | PP2 | PP3 | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Before model execution | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline | | **After model execution** | **approximately -21%** | Approximately unchanged | Approximately unchanged | Approximately unchanged | In those captured windows: - PP0 sampled-result broadcast/model-compute overlap was nearly eliminated; - recurring large PP0 gaps became one residual large gap; and - that remaining gap was dominated by pipeline `SendRecv`, not the sampled-result broadcast. PP0 improved while PP1--PP3 remained nearly unchanged, which is consistent with removing the last due-receive overlap from PP0 model execution. The result also changes the stage balance: PP2 becomes the slowest stage, so a PP partition tuned around the interfered PP0 time may need retuning after this optimization. With the previously tuned PP partition, post-model placement improved the long-generation workload by 2.4%, below the approximately 3% single-run repeatability threshold, and regressed the very-long-generation workload by 1.5%. This shows that receive placement alone is not a universal win. Both workloads reached 100% KV usage and performed repeated preemptions, so stage balance, KV capacity, and recomputation also matter. Retuning the PP partition after removing PP0 receive interference produced the following best full-window results. The comparison baseline is the earlier delay-3 configuration for each workload. The current rows combine post-model placement with PP-stage retuning; the prefill-heavy row also changes the sequence-admission limit. | Generic workload class | Change versus earlier delay-3 configuration | |---|---:| | Short generation, prefill-heavy | **approximately +11%** | | Long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +10%** | | Very long generation, decode-heavy | **approximately +5%** | The prefill-heavy configuration was repeated with receive-wait telemetry and reproduced within 0.1%. The two decode-heavy rows are single full-window results. Because the partition changed, this table must not be cited as an isolated post-model A/B. It shows that stage balancing should be repeated after receive interference is removed. This optimization should remain opt-in until it is reproduced across models, allocations, and PP sizes. ### Current source behavior At the source revision used to open this issue, [`d591d1d5`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/d591d1d511b5f2a70ae34adfd5adc5c1956ecae2): - [`PPHandler.receive()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d591d1d511b5f2a70ae34adfd5adc5c1956ecae2/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py#L126-L168) immediately posts sampled-token and count broadcasts on `broadcast_stream`; - the non-last-rank FIFO is pre-seeded with `pp_size` entries; and - [`get_prev_sampled_outputs()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d591d1d511b5f2a70ae34adfd5adc5c1956ecae2/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py#L93-L124) later consumes the slot and calls `main_stream.wait_event(slot.event)`. The delay is a local PP feedback-step cadence, not a wall-clock interval. Variable stage durations can therefore leave very different physical lead times between receive posting and consumption. ### Why a side stream is not sufficient PR #42187 correctly removes stream and communicator serialization from normal PP traffic. An unmatched receiver-side collective can nevertheless remain active while waiting for the last rank to publish its data. Closed PR [#47686](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47686) describes related early receiver-side LL-kernel spinning and proposes packing feedback fields into fewer collectives. Packing reduces the number of kernels; later receive placement reduces their lifetime. The ideas are complementary. ### Prototype implementation Draft PR [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948) adds the receiver-delay setting: ```bash VLLM_PP_DEFER_SAMPLED_TOKEN_RECV= ``` The prototype has these properties: 1. Delay `0` retains the current immediate-receive path, including stream and allocation ordering. 2. A nonzero delay requires CUDA, Model Runner V2, asynchronous scheduling, and `1 <= delay < pp_size`; invalid settings fail during configuration. 3. PP3 still posts its source broadcast immediately. Non-last ranks preserve the tensors, request-slot mapping, liveness mask, and generation snapshot, then post receives in FIFO order at `T + delay`. 4. Sender and receivers use the same skip predicate for non-final chunked prefills and requests that finish after sampling, preserving collective order and symmetry. 5. Consumption remains at `T + pp_size`. An unexpectedly unposted receive is launched defensively, and the existing event wait preserves correctness. 6. Pending receives are posted at idle boundaries and before shutdown. 7. Normal performance runs avoid event-query synchronization. Optional diagnostics measure readiness and main-stream wait time at consumption. The source can be posted before its matching receive without changing collective order, provided every participating rank executes the same FIFO of matching broadcasts and shutdown drains that FIFO before communicator destruction. The separate post-model follow-up prototype adds: ```bash VLLM_PP_POST_MODEL_SAMPLED_TOKEN_RECV=1 ``` It currently requires a nonzero receive delay and was tested with delay 3. It adds one ordering rule: when a delayed receive becomes due, launch it after the current model execution but before a boundary at which its result may be consumed, flushed, or destroyed. This setting and its implementation are not yet part of PR #53948. ### Correctness invariants and risks The implementation must preserve: - identical collective order, shape, row count, and dtype on all ranks; - association between step-`T` feedback and its saved request-slot mapping; - generation and liveness checks across abort, preemption, and slot reuse; - the existing `T + pp_size` decode-eligibility cadence; - non-final chunked-prefill behavior; - no unnecessary receive for requests that finish after the first sample; - explicit drain before shutdown or communicator destruction; and - safe CUDA-graph warmup and capture boundaries. Receiver deferral can move contention to the source rank if the source is posted much earlier than its matching receivers. Evaluation must measure both source- and receiver-side residency. Other risks include collective-order mismatch on empty steps, insufficient lead time on slower topologies, abort cleanup, and backend-specific stream/event behavior. Two historical failure modes are especially important: - independently choosing delays by PP rank broke collective FIFO order; and - delaying the source together with the receivers deadlocked. The safe baseline is therefore one common receiver delay, an immediate source, and an explicit finite drain. ### Required telemetry Performance results are difficult to interpret without aggregate counters. The opt-in diagnostic mode should report: - deferred launches; - idle-boundary flushes; - defensive consume fallbacks; - receives unready at `T + pp_size`; - total and maximum main-stream wait time at consumption; and - receives still pending at shutdown. The counters should avoid per-step logging and should not add event-query overhead to normal performance runs. ### Suggested public reproducer Use a public PP-compatible model and fixed synthetic prompts. Compare otherwise identical workloads: 1. `max_tokens=1`: the request finishes after final-prefill sampling, so no sampled result is needed for another decode step; 2. `max_tokens=2`: the first sampled token must return before the next decode step. Controls: - Model Runner V2; - `pipeline_parallel_size > 1`; - asynchronous scheduling; - fixed input length and `--ignore-eos`; - prefix caching disabled; - identical concurrency and request count; and - enough requests to exclude startup and drain effects. Compare three receiver policies while holding all other settings fixed: 1. immediate receive; 2. delayed receive before current model execution; and 3. delayed receive after current model execution. Capture Nsight Systems on at least the first and last PP ranks. Record: - receive-post time on each non-last rank; - source-post time on the last rank; - readiness at the next step and at `T + pp_size`; - time blocked by `main_stream.wait_event()`; - lifetime of the selected NCCL broadcast kernel; - overlap between that kernel and model kernels; and - model-kernel duration with and without a pending receive. ### Acceptance criteria - Identical deterministic outputs to current `main`. - No deadlock or collective mismatch during startup, steady state, empty steps, abort, preemption, finite drain, or shutdown. - Lower receiver-side NCCL/model-work overlap without harmful source-side residency. - No increase in hard-wait frequency or time at `T + pp_size`. - No material regression at low concurrency or for one-output requests. - Reproduced throughput and latency results across multiple allocations. - Validation on at least PP2 and PP4 before considering a default. ### Related upstream work - [#42187](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42187), merged: introduced the current MRV2 feedback cadence and sibling stream/process group. - [#47686](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47686), closed: proposed packing feedback fields and documented early receiver-side LL-kernel spinning. - [#50853](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50853), open RFC: broader MRV2 PP composition and deferred-result transport. - [#50410](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50410), open prototype: balances admission across PP batches; it changes work availability rather than receive placement. - [#51650](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51650), merged: overlaps sampled-token broadcast with compute on XPU. ## Report of performance regression This is not presented as a regression. PR #42187 is necessary and improves PP overlap. This proposal targets residual contention when asynchronous receives are posted substantially before source data exists. ## Misc discussion on performance The intended changes affect receiver timing only. The sampled-result dependency, collective order, consume cadence, and correctness wait remain unchanged. ## Current environment The results above used a multi-node NVIDIA GPU environment with PP4, Model Runner V2, asynchronous scheduling, and CUDA graphs. The result-provenance section names the public vLLM source revisions. A public reproducer should add sanitized `collect_env.py` output with exact CUDA, NCCL, PyTorch, and driver revisions. No private hostnames, absolute filesystem paths, scheduler identifiers, credentials, or model artifacts are included in this draft. ## Validation status - [x] Searched related public issues and PRs. - [x] Confirmed the referenced source behavior at a pinned public commit. - [x] Separated receive placement, correctness waits, and queue depth. - [x] Opened draft prototype [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948). - [x] Added focused tests for delay `0`, PP2/PP4 cadence, empty-step flushing, skip symmetry, fallback, and finite/idempotent drain. - [x] Completed end-to-end delay-3 runs with no failed benchmark requests in the three reported workloads. - [x] Measured the post-model launch variant on all three reported workloads and profiled its prefill-heavy overlap. - [x] Reproduced the best prefill-heavy combined configuration within 0.1%. - [ ] Publish the separate post-model implementation in PR #53948 or a dedicated follow-up PR. - [ ] Add a public-model synthetic reproducer. - [ ] Add sanitized `collect_env.py` output and public trace attachments. - [ ] Repeat the same-allocation prefill-heavy post-model A/B. - [ ] Validate GPU execution on PP2 and on current `main` before proposing an upstream default.

hits.title: [Bug]: extract_hidden_states uses first-column feedback for multi-token outputs

### Your current environment
